cards.name: Inverted Row
cards.doThisNotThat: Pull your chest to the edge as one rigid plank, with heels down and glutes squeezed, and lead with the elbows driving toward your back pockets. Most people sag at the hips and crane the chin up, so the reps "count" without the back doing the work.
cards.priorityNote: At home this is your main horizontal pull (no pull-up bar). Athleticism and posture win here, so keep the body rigid even if that means fewer reps; looks follow.

prescription.reps: 6-12 (double progression: 12 clean on all sets → feet onto a chair, then add a 2-s hold at the top)
prescription.load: Bodyweight; set the difficulty with body angle. More horizontal = harder. Stop at 1-2 RIR or when the hips start to sag.
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lower, 1-s hold with chest at the edge, explosive pull
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day, main lift at home (or the first accessory in the gym after pull-ups)
prescription.warmup: 1 set x 6 at a steeper (easier) angle

steps: Use a heavy, stable table that cannot tip (test it first, or have someone sit on it). Lie underneath with your chest under the edge.
Grip the edge just wider than shoulders, palms facing away, thumbs wrapped.
Heels on the floor, legs straight, glutes squeezed, ribs down: shoulders to ankles is one straight line.
Pull the chest to the edge, hold 1 s, lower until the arms are fully straight and the shoulder blades spread.
cues: Pull the table edge to your sternum.
Drive your elbows toward your back pockets.
Keep your belt buckle pointed at the ceiling.

biomechanics.forceVector: Mostly horizontal pull. The more horizontal your body, the larger the share of bodyweight you lift (roughly 50-70% of bodyweight in common setups).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder extension from ~90° flexion to ~0-10° behind the torso; elbows ~45° from the body; scapulae retract and depress at the top.
biomechanics.momentArm: The body is a lever pivoting on the heels; the arms pull near the top of the lever. Feet elevated moves the pivot up and raises the load share.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Heels → glutes → anti-extension brace → scapulae → elbows. If the plank breaks, force leaks into the hips instead of the back.
biomechanics.grf: Heels push into the floor and act as the pivot; push the heels down to lock the plank so pulling force goes into moving the body, not bending it.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Top 20% (chest to the edge), where the moment arm on the lats and mid-back is greatest and the shoulder blades must fully retract.

neural.intent: Explode up, control down. Pull fast and hard every rep; slow reps at the top mean you stop the set.
neural.rfd: Moderate. Fast pulling RFD is the same rate you need to snap back the hand after a jab or pull a collar tie.

powerPair.exercise: Explosive inverted row with a hand release (let go at the top, catch the edge)
powerPair.rest: 20-30 s after the main set

cards.mobility: Full arm extension at the bottom with the shoulder blades spread loads the lats and rhomboids long, opening the upper back your posture rounds. The loaded range builds mobility about as well as stretching (Afonso 2021).
cards.footBase: Heels are the base: pressing them into the floor locks the posterior chain, so the plank stays rigid. Feet together, toes up.
cards.sequencing: Scapula first, then elbows: the shoulder blades start the pull and the arms finish it. That is the same order your boxing guard returns in.

looks.effect: Mid-back thickness, rear delts and posture. You stand taller, and the V-taper reads better from the side.
looks.lengthened: Bottom: arms straight, shoulder blades spread wide, 1-s stretch before each rep. Last set: 3-5 bottom-half partials.

sportTransfer.mechanism: The retraction strength balances all the pushing and punching, which keeps the shoulder centered. A strong horizontal pull also decelerates the arm after throws and serves.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Clinch pulls, pulling an opponent into a knee, and fast jab retraction. Also counters the forward-rounded "boxer posture".

intensityTechnique.technique: Rest-pause: at 1 RIR, rest 15 s, do 2-3 more reps, repeat once

tips.tip: Change difficulty by angle, not by ugly reps. Walk the feet forward or put them on a chair to progress. A 1-s top hold doubles time at the hardest point with zero new equipment.

Stop when the hips start to sag. That is your velocity-loss cue at home; grinding past it trains a broken plank, and stopping early kept more speed in velocity-loss studies (Pareja-Blanco 2017 — squat data, extrapolated).
Do a horizontal pull for every push. Matching the volume protects the front of the shoulder, which takes a lot of stress from punching volume.
Safety: test the table. It must be heavy and not tip. A sturdy bar in a rack, or a broomstick between two chairs (backs together, with weight on them), also works. Avoid flimsy furniture.

cards.teachMe: Your back muscles pull the shoulder blades together first, and then the arms finish the job. When the arms go first (your usual pattern), the biceps work hard and the back does little. The heels act as a pivot: you are a lever being pulled up, so a rigid plank lets all the force move your body instead of bending it at the hips. Training that full chain at once teaches your nervous system to fire the trunk and the back as one unit, which is the same stiffness that makes a punch transfer force.

swaps.home: Table inverted row (above), or a sturdy broom across two heavy chairs. If neither works: towel door rows (towel around both handles of a closed door, lean back, pull) or a one-arm DB row.
swaps.bodyweight: Door-frame or towel-door row, feet close to the door and body leaning back; walk the feet forward to make it harder.

cards.name: Dumbbell Pullover
cards.doThisNotThat: Keep the elbows soft and locked at one angle, ribs pulled down, and lower the DB behind your head only as far as your ribs stay down. Then drag it back over your eyes with the lats. Most people bend and straighten the elbows (turning it into a skull crusher) and arch the low back to fake range.
cards.priorityNote: Looks (lat width for the V-taper) and shoulder mobility win; the main lift remains the row or pull-up.

prescription.reps: 10-15 (double progression: 15 on all sets → +5 lb or 3-s lowering)
prescription.load: 1-2 RIR, failure on the last set. One light-moderate DB held with both hands.
prescription.tempo: 3 s lower to the stretch, 1-s pause, pull up hard to above the eyes
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day, accessory (after rows; before triceps work)

steps: Lie with your upper back across a bench (or flat on the floor at home), feet flat in a tripod, hips level.
Hold one DB with both hands cupped under the top plate, arms straight up over the chest, elbows slightly bent.
Exhale, pull ribs down. Lower the DB in an arc behind the head until you feel a big stretch in your lats, without the ribs flaring.
Pause 1 s, then pull the DB back up in the same arc until it's above the eyes (not over the chest).
cues: Draw a big arc with the dumbbell — same elbow angle the whole time.
Keep your bottom ribs pinned to the bench.
Drag the dumbbell back over your eyes, not your chest.

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls down while the arm moves in an arc around the shoulder, so the load on the lats is greatest when the arm is near horizontal behind the head.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder flexion ~90° → ~160-180° (overhead); elbows locked at ~10-20° bend. The lat is longest with the arm overhead.
biomechanics.momentArm: Max when the arm is horizontal (DB furthest from the shoulder horizontally), which is also near the stretch position: hard and long at the same time.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Ribs down (abs) → shoulder blades on the bench → the arm swings around the shoulder. Lose the ribs and the lumbar spine makes the range instead of the shoulder.
biomechanics.grf: Feet push into the floor to keep the hips stable; minimal role otherwise.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Arm near horizontal behind the head, which is also the lengthened part of the range.

neural.intent: Controlled stretch, then pull with intent. Feel the lats start the arc, not the triceps.
neural.rfd: Low priority. This is a range-and-looks lift.

cards.mobility: The best overhead-mobility tool in the program. It loads the lats and long head of the triceps in full shoulder flexion with the ribs down, which is the range stiff lats steal (it forces the back to arch when you reach overhead). Loaded ROM ≈ stretching for range (Afonso 2021).
cards.footBase: Tripod feet flat and wide on the floor; light Screw pressure to keep the pelvis level so the back doesn't arch.

looks.effect: Lat width and serratus definition, which together make the V-taper. Also some upper-chest fill.
looks.lengthened: The stretch with the arm overhead, ribs down. Last set: 5-6 partials in the bottom (overhead) third only.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Overhead range without the low back arching protects the spine in serves, spikes, throws and rebounds. Stronger lats in the stretched position drive the "pull down" of a spike or overhead serve.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Overhook and whizzer strength, frames in BJJ, and a long overhand reach without the ribs flaring.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials (5-6 in the overhead third)

tips.tip: Ribs down is the whole lift. When the ribs flare, the lumbar spine gives the "fake" overhead range, and the lats stay short. Exhale fully before each rep.
The lat is longest overhead. Training at long lengths often grows muscle at least as well as full ROM (Wolf 2023 meta; parity in Wolf 2025), so the stretch here is a free bonus.
Stop the up-arc above the eyes. Past that point gravity has no lever on the lats, so it's a rest instead of a rep.
Cross-bench (shoulders on the bench, hips lower) gives the most range; flat on the floor is safer if your shoulders are stiff and you want the floor to stop the range for you.

cards.teachMe: Stiff lats are a hidden reason you cannot reach overhead without arching your back. The lats attach to the arm and the low back, so when they are short, raising the arm pulls the spine into an arch. Loading the stretch with the ribs held down teaches your nervous system the overhead position is safe, and it releases the protective tension, so range shows up in your serve, your shot and your guard. The physics: the load is hardest exactly when the lat is longest, so this is one of the few exercises where hard and stretched happen together.

swaps.home: Floor DB pullover with the light DB; the floor limits range safely. If it's too light, use a 4-s lowering and lengthened partials.
swaps.bodyweight: Towel lat slide: kneel or plank with hands on a towel on a smooth floor, slide the arms overhead and pull back with the lats (ab-wheel style but short range).

cards.name: Prone Y-T-W Raise
cards.doThisNotThat: Lift from the shoulder blades with the thumbs pointed up and the neck long, and hold each top position 2 s. Most people heave with the low back, shrug the upper traps and flap the arms, so the weak lower traps never do any work.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism (shoulder health for punching and throwing volume) wins over looks. Small, precise, light.

prescription.reps: 8 each of Y, T and W (24 total per round), 2-s hold at the top of each rep
prescription.load: Bodyweight to 2-5 lb. If the upper traps take over or you shrug, the weight is too heavy.
prescription.tempo: 1 s up, 2-s hold, 2 s down
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day accessory; also a pre-press warm-up (1 round with no weight) on Chest days, and before boxing
prescription.warmup: No warm-up set needed; the first round is light enough to warm up

steps: Lie face-down on the floor (forehead on a folded towel) or chest-down on a 30-45° incline bench.
Y: arms overhead at ~135° (a Y shape), thumbs up. T: arms out at 90°, thumbs up. W: elbows bent and tucked, pull them toward the back pockets, thumbs up.
Lift the arms a few inches off the floor by sliding the shoulder blades down and together; hold 2 s.
Lower slowly. Keep the chin tucked and the lower ribs on the floor.
cues: Point your thumbs at the ceiling.
Slide your shoulder blades into your back pockets.
Keep your forehead on the towel.

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls the arms down; the scapular muscles lift them against it. In the Y the line of pull matches the lower traps' fibers; in the T the mid traps; in the W the rotator cuff (external rotation) and rhomboids.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Y: ~135° shoulder abduction-flexion; T: 90° abduction; W: ~45° abduction with 90° elbow bend and external rotation. Thumbs up = external rotation, which opens space at the front of the shoulder.
biomechanics.momentArm: Long straight arms in Y and T give a big lever, so even 2 lb is hard. The W shortens the lever, which allows slightly more load.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Scapula moves first (down and back), then the arm. If the arm moves without the scapula, the upper traps and rear delt take over.
biomechanics.grf: Minimal: the floor or bench supports the torso, which removes low-back cheating if the ribs stay down.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The top hold in the Y, where the lower traps are fully shortened against the longest lever.

neural.intent: Precise, slow and owned: this is motor control, not power. You are teaching the brain to find the lower traps on demand.
neural.rfd: Not a target.

cards.mobility: Overhead range (Y) with the ribs down and the thumbs-up external rotation (W) restore range that stiff, rounded shoulders lose. Light, end-range loading builds active control there, which is what the brain needs before it lets the joint move.
cards.sequencing: Scapula first, then the arm. Stabilizing the shoulder blade before the arm moves is the base for punching, throwing and serving: the hips start the punch, but the scapula is the platform the arm fires from.

looks.effect: Posture (shoulders back, chest up), rear-delt detail and an upper back that "frames" the shoulders, so the V-taper reads from the front and side.
looks.lengthened: Let the shoulder blades spread fully at the bottom of each rep before lifting.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Lower traps and the cuff decelerate the arm after punches, throws, serves and spikes. That braking capacity protects the shoulder when volume is high.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Hundreds of punches a week pull the shoulders forward. This counters the boxer slouch, keeps the guard high longer before fatigue, and protects the shoulder in snapping punches and frames.

intensityTechnique.technique: Iso-hold finisher: 20 s in the top Y position after the last round

tips.tip: Weight is not progress here: add hold time (2 s → 5 s) or reps before adding even 2 lb. The moment the upper traps shrug, the exercise has changed muscles.
Thumbs up (external rotation) keeps the front of the shoulder open when the arm is raised. Thumbs down closes that space and can pinch.
Put 1 round before pressing and boxing as a primer. Light activation helps the scapula set in its best position before load, so pressing feels steadier.
External cue wins: "thumbs to the ceiling" beats "squeeze your lower traps" for performance and learning (Wulf).

cards.teachMe: Your nervous system protects shoulders it doesn't trust: weak lower traps make the brain clamp the upper traps and limit how hard you can punch or throw. Small, precise holds at the end of the range build a map of the shoulder blade in the brain, so the platform the arm fires from stays steady when you snap a jab or serve. Steady base, more force out: the same Newton's 3rd law as the floor under your feet, applied to the shoulder blade.

swaps.home: Floor Y-T-W, bodyweight or with water bottles (~1 lb). Progress by holding longer at the top.
swaps.bodyweight: Floor Y-T-W with no load; or wall slides with the forearms on a wall, sliding up into a Y.

cards.name: Sprawl
cards.doThisNotThat: Shoot the hips back and DOWN to the mat with the legs splayed wide on the toes, chest heavy, then snap back to stance with hands up. Most people do a lazy burpee: they drop the knees, land with flat feet together, and stand up with hands down.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism (reactive hip speed and fight conditioning) wins. Done as a skill drill first, conditioning second; quality stops the set, not a rep count.

prescription.reps: Skill: 3 x 6 reactive sprawls (on a sibling's clap or a random cue). Conditioning: 20-30 s on / 30-40 s off
prescription.load: Bodyweight. Stop the round when the recovery to stance slows, or the hands drop at the top.
prescription.rest: Skill: 60-90 s. Conditioning: per the interval
prescription.tempo: Explosive drop, 1-s heavy hips on the mat, explosive recover
prescription.slot: Fight Lab / Boxing conditioning finisher, or after shadowboxing rounds; contact ladder level 0 (solo) or 2 (cooperative: sibling shoots slowly, you sprawl)
prescription.warmup: 1 slow-motion set of 3 to groove the pattern

steps: Start in fight stance: knees ~25° bent, hip hinge ~15°, hands up, weight on the balls of the feet.
On the cue: throw the legs back and wide, drive the hips down to the mat; land on the balls of the feet with the hands hitting the floor (or the opponent's back).
Hips heavy, chest heavy, head up; hold 1 s.
Snap the feet back under you in one hop and land in stance with the hands up. Step-and-Stick: freeze 1 s balanced.
cues: Throw your hips to the floor behind you.
Feet go wide like a kickstand.
Land back in stance with your hands at your cheekbones.

biomechanics.forceVector: Hips move backward and down fast; gravity plus active hip extension drive body mass onto the opponent's head and shoulders (or the mat).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hips go from ~60° flexion in stance to ~0° (or extended) on the mat; legs ~shoulder width-plus apart; ankles dorsiflexed on the toes.
biomechanics.momentArm: Wide feet make a broad base and lower the center of mass, which makes it far harder for an opponent to turn the corner on you.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Eyes see the shot → hips fire back → core braces → arms post/frame. Hips first: if the arms reach first, you get dragged into the takedown.
biomechanics.grf: On the recovery, the balls of the feet push into the floor to drive the hips forward and up into stance. Newton's 3rd: the push into the floor is what brings you back up.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The recovery from the mat to stance, especially with fatigue.

neural.intent: React, then explode. The drop is a reaction to a visual or sound cue, which trains the eyes-to-hips connection.
neural.rfd: High. A sprawl that lands 0.2 s late is a takedown, so the drop must be as fast as possible.

powerPair.rest: 20-30 s after a sprawl set

cards.elastic: The recovery hop uses a small stretch-shortening cycle at the ankle and hip. Land on the balls of the feet and rebound instead of stepping back one foot at a time.
cards.mobility: Hip extension through the sprawl stretches the hip flexors (which stay short from sitting) under a dynamic load.
cards.footBase: In stance and on the recovery landing: tripod foot and the Screw, so the arches hold, the knees stay out, and the stance is stable. On the mat: balls of the feet with toes tucked under, not tops of the feet.
cards.sequencing: Hips lead, hands follow. The hips get back and down before the hands touch, the same hips-first order as every punch and throw. Arm-first = getting taken down.

looks.effect: Conditioning and leanness without any deficit; some chest, shoulder and core tone from the repeated drops.
looks.lengthened: Hip flexors are lengthened in the bottom of the sprawl.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Reacting to a visual cue and moving the hips fast is the same skill as reacting to a cut on defense in basketball, a tackle in football, or a change of direction in soccer.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Core takedown defense. Wrestle at contact ladder level 0 (solo) or 2 (sibling shoots slowly, you sprawl, no driving through); never live with a younger sibling.

intensityTechnique.technique: Reactive cue rounds: random clap/visual cue, 20-30 s

tips.tip: Use a reaction cue (clap, finger point, phone flashing) instead of doing them on your own rhythm. Reacting to a stimulus trains the eyes-to-hips link; your own rhythm trains only fitness.
Stop the round when recovery to stance slows or the hands drop at the top. A sloppy sprawl rehearsed is a bad habit rehearsed.

Sprawl rounds are conditioning. If you have asthma, warm up with intervals (e.g. 8 x 30 s hard / 30 s easy) 15-30 min before; high-intensity interval warm-ups reduced the post-exercise lung function drop (Stickland 2012).
Freeze 1 s in stance on every recovery (Step-and-Stick). The pause installs balance at the end of the movement, which is when fighters get hit.

cards.teachMe: A takedown attempt is a fast visual threat. If your brain is in threat mode, you freeze and react late, and that is the whole fight. Sprawling to a random cue teaches the system to turn "see shot" into "hips back" without thinking, so the reaction becomes automatic. The physics: wide feet and low hips mean a big base and low center of mass, so the attacker has to lift your weight against gravity instead of you falling into them.

swaps.home: Same drill on a rug or mat in the living room; sibling claps or points as the cue (level 0-2).
swaps.bodyweight: Same: it's already bodyweight. Easier version: sprawl to the knees on a soft surface, then build to the full sprawl.

cards.name: Treadmill Sprint
cards.doThisNotThat: Sprint on a 6-10% incline with short, fast reps (8-12 s) and full recovery, after a proper interval warm-up. Most people run flat-out on a flat belt for 30+ s with short rest, which is conditioning sludge with more hamstring risk and no top-speed training.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism (speed and power) wins. These are speed reps, not conditioning, so keep rest long; if rep 5 is slower than rep 1, stop.

prescription.load: Incline 6-10%, belt speed set so you can hold near-max for 8-12 s (start ~9-11 mph and adjust). Step off onto the side rails between reps.
prescription.rest: 60-90 s walking between reps (straddle the rails); full recovery on top-speed days
prescription.tempo: Max intent each rep
prescription.slot: Sprint/speed day or after CNS prime before lifting legs; never after heavy leg training
prescription.warmup: EIB interval warm-up: 5 min easy jog → 8 x 30 s fast / 30 s easy (~15 min before the first sprint), then pogos 2 x 15 and 3 build-ups at 70/80/90%

steps: Do the EIB interval warm-up (above) about 15-30 min before the main sprints. If you have a prescribed pre-exercise inhaler, use it the way your doctor set up.
Set incline to 6-10%. Stand on the side rails, set the speed, hold the handrails and step on when the belt is at speed.
Let go of the rails immediately: tall posture, slight forward lean from the ankles, arms driving.
After 8-12 s, grab the rails and step back to the side; walk or rest 60-90 s.
cues: Punch the belt down and back under your hips.
Drive your knee toward the screen.
Swing your hands from hip pocket to chin.

biomechanics.forceVector: Mostly vertical force into the belt with a backward push; on an incline, the push line tilts so the hips must extend harder. Top speed depends on how much vertical force you put into the ground in a short contact.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Knee lift to ~90° hip flexion, foot strikes close under the hip; at the end of the push, hip extended near 0-10°. Incline shortens the stride slightly, reducing the hamstring's end-of-swing stretch.
biomechanics.momentArm: Foot landing far in front of the hip (overstriding) creates a braking moment and loads the hamstring at its longest. Landing under the hip keeps the lever short.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Ground → ankle (stiff spring) → knee → hip extension → trunk stays tall → arms counterbalance the legs.
biomechanics.grf: Short, hard contacts: push the belt down and back. Newton's 3rd: the harder you push into the belt in a short contact, the more it pushes you up and forward.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Late swing, when the hamstring decelerates the lower leg before foot strike. Incline reduces the speed of that phase and the risk.

neural.intent: Max intent, relaxed face and hands. Tension in the face spreads to the shoulders and slows the arm swing.
neural.rfd: Very high: ground contacts at speed are ~0.1-0.2 s, so force must be produced faster than you can think.

powerPair.rest: ~3-4 min before the first sprint (part of the warm-up)

cards.elastic: Your Achilles is the spring: stiff ankles and short contacts store and return energy. Pogos before the sprints tune the spring.
cards.mobility: Full hip extension in each push stretches the hip flexors at high speed; full knee drive works hip flexion range dynamically.
cards.footBase: Land on the ball of the foot under the hip with the arch braced (short-foot under the foot). A collapsing arch leaks force and lets the knee cave; strong ankles and pogos help you hold it.
cards.sequencing: Arms and legs counterbalance: the opposite arm drives back as the leg pushes. A tight upper body and a relaxed face let the arm swing match the legs.

looks.effect: Hamstrings, glutes and calves, and leanness without a deficit. Sprinters are lean and muscular because the work is short and intense.
looks.lengthened: Hamstrings and hip flexors are lengthened at high speed in each stride.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Acceleration and top speed in every running sport; short contacts and a stiff ankle improve XC running economy too.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Topuria-style engine: roadwork plus sprints. Short sprints build the fast-twitch power for explosive exchanges without slowing you down.

intensityTechnique.technique: Velocity-loss cutoff: stop the session when a rep is visibly slower than the first

tips.tip: The interval warm-up matters for your lungs: high-intensity interval and variable-intensity warm-ups reduced the post-exercise drop in lung function (FEV1), while continuous easy jogging didn't reliably help. About half of asthmatics get a refractory window of about 1-2 h.
HR targets: max HR ~200-205. Warm-up intervals ~160-180 bpm (80-88%). Sprints are too short for HR to tell you much; use rep speed instead.
Incline sprints cut top speed and overstriding, which lowers the hamstring's end-of-swing stress, a safer way to sprint hard while you build up to flat sprints.

Stop when a rep is slower than the first. Stopping before speed drops preserved more power and gave bigger jump gains in lifting (Pareja-Blanco 2017, VL20 vs VL40) — the same logic applies to sprints.
Nordic hamstring curls (2 x 4-6, 1-2x/week) are the best insurance for sprinting: programs including them cut hamstring injuries by up to ~51% (van Dyk 2019).
Treadmill safety: start and stop from the side rails; never jump on a moving belt; clip the safety key on.

cards.teachMe: Speed is mostly how much force you put into the ground in a tiny window: about a tenth of a second per step. That is faster than conscious thought, so the nervous system has to learn it, which is why you sprint fresh, short and fast, never tired. Your lungs need the interval warm-up because a fast jump into heavy breathing dries and cools your airways, which can trigger narrowing; short hard bursts first can leave your airways less reactive for a while. Incline reduces how far your leg reaches in front of you, so the hamstring has to brake less, letting you sprint hard with less risk.

swaps.home: Treadmill incline sprints (as above), or outdoors: hill sprints 6-8 x 8-12 s at a 5-10% hill, walk back down for rest.
swaps.bodyweight: Hill sprints or flat sprints of 10-20 m in a park; in a small space, A-skips and fast high knees for 8-10 s.

cards.name: Norwegian 4x4 Intervals
cards.doThisNotThat: Run each 4-minute interval at a pace that brings HR to 85-95% of max (≈172-195 bpm for you) by minute 2-3 and hold it there, after an interval warm-up for your airways. Most people sprint the first minute, then die. That front-loads lactate and you never accumulate time near VO2 max.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism (engine for XC, fighting and all your sports) wins. Once a week only; it is hard on the system, so keep it away from heavy leg days and game days.

prescription.reps: 4 min hard at 85-95% HRmax (≈172-195 bpm) + 3 min active recovery at ~60-70% (≈120-140 bpm) between
prescription.load: Speed/incline that gets HR to ~172+ by minute 2-3; last minute of each interval ~185-195. Should feel like 8/10 effort, not an all-out sprint.
prescription.rest: 3 min active recovery (easy jog/walk) between intervals
prescription.tempo: Even pace, slightly faster in the last minute
prescription.slot: VO2 Day (once a week); not within 48 h of a game or fight; not the day before heavy legs
prescription.warmup: EIB interval warm-up: 5 min easy → 6-8 x 30 s fast / 30 s easy (~15-20 min before interval 1), then 3-5 min easy. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler the way your doctor set up.

steps: Do the interval warm-up, then 3-5 min easy jog.
Interval 1: set speed/incline so HR climbs to ~172 by minute 2-3. Treadmill: incline 2-6% lets you hit HR at a lower belt speed.
Recovery: drop to easy jog/walk for 3 min; HR should fall toward ~130-140.
Repeat 4 times. Cooldown 5-10 min easy, nasal breathing if you can.
cues: Run tall like a string is pulling your head to the ceiling.
Quick, quiet feet — 170-180 steps per minute, in time to the music.
Breathe out long through the mouth at the hard part.

biomechanics.forceVector: Repeated vertical push into the belt at moderate force; the goal is economy: minimal braking, minimal bounce.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Foot lands under the hip with a slight knee bend; cadence 170-180 keeps contacts short and avoids overstriding.
biomechanics.momentArm: Overstriding puts the foot far in front of the hip, which acts as a brake every step; a short stride under the hips reduces that braking moment.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Stiff ankle spring → knee → hip extension → tall trunk → relaxed arms in rhythm with the legs.
biomechanics.grf: Push the belt down and back each step. Newton's 3rd: the belt pushes you up and forward; wasted vertical bounce is energy lost.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Minutes 3-4 of intervals 3 and 4, when HR is near max and form breaks.

neural.intent: Steady, controlled hard effort. This is an engine session; save explosive intent for other days.
neural.rfd: Not a target.

cards.elastic: Running economy uses the Achilles spring: short contacts at 170-180 steps/min and stiff ankles return energy. Pogos 2 x 15 before the warm-up tune the spring.
cards.mobility: Running through full hip extension each stride works the hip flexors dynamically; the cooldown is the time for slow nasal breathing and light hip-flexor stretching.
cards.footBase: Short-foot under each landing, ankle stiff, foot landing under the hip. Collapsed arches let the knee cave on every step, thousands of times — that leaks energy and stresses the knee.
cards.sequencing: Arms counterbalance the legs: elbow drives back as the opposite leg pushes. Relaxed shoulders and hands keep the rhythm smooth.

looks.effect: Leanness and heart health without dieting; the session builds the engine, it does not shrink muscle at once-a-week volume.
looks.lengthened: Not a looks lift.

sportTransfer.mechanism: A bigger VO2 max lets you work at a higher pace before you go into the red, and recover faster between sprints, points and rounds. Your ~173 bpm at 8:22/mile shows the engine is the limiter.
sportTransfer.combatNote: A bigger engine lets you hold the 70% sustainable pace (Zahabi) longer and recover between exchanges; it is the "roadwork" half of Topuria's roadwork + sprints.

intensityTechnique.technique: Progressive last minute: speed up so the final minute of each interval hits ~185-195 bpm

tips.tip: Do the interval warm-up 15-30 min before interval 1: high-intensity and variable-intensity warm-ups reduced the post-exercise lung-function drop in EIB; continuous easy jogging alone didn't reliably help (Stickland 2012).
Sync music to 170-180 BPM: running in time to music lowered oxygen cost and extended time to exhaustion in triathletes (Terry 2012).

Script 3 lines of self-talk for minute 3-4 of the hard intervals ("smooth and strong", "push the belt", "one more minute"). Motivational self-talk lowered effort ratings and extended time to exhaustion (Blanchfield 2014).
Judge by HR, not speed: your HR runs naturally high, so use your Garmin. If you can't reach ~172 by minute 3, raise incline, not speed.
No cold bath after a lifting day, but cold water after conditioning like this is fine (Roberts 2015 blunted gains only after strength training).

cards.teachMe: VO2 max is the most oxygen your body can use per minute, and the heart's output is the main limiter. Four minutes is long enough to spend most of the interval near max heart rate, which is the signal that grows the heart's stroke volume. The airway warm-up exists because heavy, fast breathing dries and cools your airways, and short hard bursts first often leave them less reactive for a couple of hours. Cadence matters: shorter, quicker steps reduce braking forces every stride, so the same speed costs less oxygen.

swaps.home: Treadmill as prescribed. Use incline (2-6%) to hit HR at a lower speed if top speed is limited.
swaps.bodyweight: Outdoor hill or flat-road run at the same HR targets; or, no space: 4 x 4 min of shadowboxing + jumping jacks + high knees at HR 172+ (harder to hit the HR, so check your Garmin).

cards.name: Barbell Back Squat
cards.doThisNotThat: Screw your feet into the floor and drive the floor away fast out of the hole — don't sit back, collapse the arches, and grind slow reps to failure.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism > looks: reps stop when bar speed visibly drops, even if you could grind 2 more for size.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; end the set when a rep visibly slows (~20% velocity loss)
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s down, 0 s pause, max-intent up
prescription.slot: Main lift #1 on Legs day, after CNS prime
prescription.warmup: 1 set x 5 at ~50-60% of working load, same max-intent speed

steps: Safeties set 2-3 cm below your bottom position — non-negotiable if you train alone.
Bar on upper traps, hands just outside shoulders, elbows under the bar, not flared back.
Feet shoulder-width, toes out 15-30°. Tripod down (big toe, pinky toe, heel), then screw the feet out until the arches rise.
Big breath into the belly and sides, brace like you're about to take a body shot, unrack, 2 steps back.
cues: Spread the floor apart
Push the floor through the ceiling
Knees track over the 2nd-3rd toe

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical. The bar path should stay over mid-foot; any drift forward turns it into a good-morning and loads the back instead of the legs.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Depth: hip crease at or just below knee top. Knee flexion ~110-125°, trunk lean ~30-45° from vertical (high-bar), shin angle ~30-35° forward.
biomechanics.momentArm: Hip moment arm grows with trunk lean; knee moment arm grows as knees travel forward. Knees forward past toes is fine — it shifts load to quads, which is what you want for jumping.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot → ankle → knee → hip → trunk brace → bar. Arch collapse at the bottom lets the knee cave, which leaks force sideways before it reaches the hip.
biomechanics.grf: Newton's 3rd: push the earth down and it pushes you up with equal force. Push straight down through the whole tripod and the force travels up the chain; push through the inner edge of the foot and it bends the knee inward.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Just above parallel (the sticking region) where the quad's leverage is worst and the knee moment arm is near its maximum.

neural.intent: Control the descent for 2-3 s, then try to throw the bar off your back on every rep even when it moves slowly. Intent recruits high-threshold motor units.
neural.rfd: Rate of force development comes from how fast you reverse at the bottom. A relaxed but tight bounce out of the hole (no stopping dead) uses the stretch reflex.

powerPair.rest: Do the jumps 4-6 min after the last heavy set (PAPE window); 2 min between jumps

cards.mobility: A full-depth squat under load is a loaded ankle-dorsiflexion and hip-flexion stretch. Doing 2-3 s controlled descents teaches your nervous system that the bottom position is safe, so it stops guarding and you gain depth over weeks. Full-ROM strength training improves ROM about as well as stretching (Afonso 2021).
cards.footBase: Flat feet are the main leak. Tripod first, then the Screw: rotate both feet outward against the floor without letting them move. The arch lifts, glutes switch on, knees line up. If your arch collapses at the bottom, the load is too heavy for your base. Drop 10% until it holds.
cards.sequencing: Out of the hole, hips and chest rise together at the same rate. If the hips shoot up first, the quads quit and the back takes over.

looks.effect: Quads (especially vastus lateralis/medialis) and glutes: fuller legs that match the upper body.
looks.lengthened: The quads are most stretched in the deepest third. Full depth plus 2-3 bottom-half partials after the last full rep biases distal quad growth (Pedrosa 2022).

sportTransfer.mechanism: Bigger maximal leg force raises the ceiling for jump and sprint force. Heavy strength work plus plyos improves running economy for XC (Balsalobre-Fernández 2016).
sportTransfer.combatNote: The squat's bottom position is your level change for a double leg. A strong, stable bottom means you can drop and drive without your knees caving.

intensityTechnique.technique: None on heavy sets. Failure costs speed and recovery. Optional: 1 back-off set of 8 at -15% with 2-3 bottom-half lengthened partials.
intensityTechnique.when: Back-off set only, and only if you have no game within 48 h

tips.tip: Stop the set when rep speed visibly drops. In Pareja-Blanco 2017, sets stopped at 20% velocity loss improved CMJ 9.5% vs 3.5% for 40% velocity loss, despite 40% fewer reps.
Rest the full 3 min. In trained men, 3 min rest built more strength and quad thickness than 1 min.
Squatting doesn't spike hormones that grow your arms. That old claim is not supported. Squat for legs, jumping, and sprinting.
Film one set from the side each week. If the bar drifts forward of mid-foot at the bottom, your ankles are limiting you. Use 1-2 cm heel plates temporarily while dorsiflexion improves.
Exhale only after passing the sticking point. Letting your air out at the bottom collapses the brace and the spine absorbs the force.

cards.teachMe: Your brain sets a speed limit based on how stable it thinks you are. When your arches collapse and your knees wobble, it detects instability and slows down the rate it fires muscle. Screwing the feet into the floor gives the brain a solid base, so it releases more force. Think of the squat as a way to push the earth away, not as lifting a bar.

swaps.home: Goblet or front-rack DB Bulgarian split squat, 3 s down, 1 s pause in the hole, 6-10 reps per leg. Split stance doubles the load per leg with light DBs.
swaps.bodyweight: Heels-elevated slow squat (4 s down, 2 s pause) for 12-20, then 1-2 jump squats per set to keep the power.

cards.name: Goblet Squat
cards.doThisNotThat: Use the weight as a counterbalance to sit deep and upright with a 3 s descent and a 2 s pause. Don't rush shallow reps with a weight too light to matter.
cards.priorityNote: Mobility and position quality first; this is a base-building tool, not a max-strength lift.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR
prescription.tempo: 3 s down, 2 s pause at the bottom, fast up
prescription.slot: Main lift on home Legs day, or a warm-up primer before back squats
prescription.warmup: 1 x 8 bodyweight with a 3 s pause at the bottom, elbows pushing knees out

steps: Hold one DB vertically at the chest, hands cupping the top head, elbows pointing down.
Feet slightly wider than shoulders, toes out 20-30°.
Tripod down, screw the feet out, breathe and brace, then descend between your heels.
cues: Elbows slide inside the knees
Sit between your heels
Chest stays facing the wall in front

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical. The front load moves your centre of mass forward, so you can stay upright and reach depth with less ankle demand.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Trunk ~15-25° from vertical, full knee flexion ~130°+, hips below knees.
biomechanics.momentArm: Upright trunk keeps the hip moment arm short and moves the work to the knees. That makes it quad-dominant and easier on the back.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot tripod → knee over toes → hip → braced trunk → arms holding the bell close.
biomechanics.grf: Push the floor away evenly through all three foot points. Feel the pressure move from mid-foot toward the whole foot as you stand.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The bottom 10 cm out of the pause, where the stretch reflex has gone.

neural.intent: Slow descent to teach the position, then stand up as fast as possible.
neural.rfd: Pausing removes the bounce, so the drive is pure concentric starting strength. That builds your first-step burst from a dead stop.

powerPair.exercise: Squat jump (hands on hips, stick the landing)
powerPair.rest: 20-30 s after each goblet set

cards.mobility: The best tool in the program for your stiffness. A 2 s pause at full depth with the elbows prying the knees out is a loaded hip-opener and ankle stretch. Add 20-30 s of rocking in the bottom on the last set.
cards.footBase: Watch your feet in the bottom. Flat feet will roll the arch in and drop the knees. Keep the big-toe ball heavy and screw outward, and you'll feel the glutes switch on and the arch rise. Do it barefoot at home for extra foot muscle work.

looks.effect: Quads and adductors; good volume builder when you only have light dumbbells.
looks.lengthened: The deep pause puts the quads and adductors under load at long length, the most growth-friendly part of the range.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Owning a deep, upright, braced position transfers to staying low on defense, low volleys in pickleball and tennis, and getting your hips under you.
sportTransfer.combatNote: A deep upright squat is the wrestling stance under load. If you can hold it with the arches up, your shots and sprawls come from a stable base.

intensityTechnique.technique: 1½ reps (down, halfway up, back down, then up) on the last set
intensityTechnique.when: Last set only; with light home DBs, use it on all sets

tips.tip: With light DBs, make the set hard through time and range: 3 s down plus a 2 s pause. Growth is similar across a wide band of loads when you finish close to failure.
Rep duration between 0.5 and 8 s grows muscle similarly. Pauses here are for position and stability, not as a hypertrophy trick.
Strength training through full range improves ROM about as well as stretching. This counts as mobility work.
Do it barefoot at home. Without a cushioned shoe your foot muscles have to hold the arch, which is the short-foot work your flat feet need under real load.

cards.teachMe: Your nervous system protects positions it doesn't trust by tightening the muscles around them. A slow, loaded pause at the bottom shows your brain that this range is safe, so it stops guarding and lets you go deeper. Your mobility improves because your nervous system relaxes, not because tissue stretches like a rubber band.

swaps.home: This is the home swap. Use the heaviest DB you have; if it's too light, switch to heels-elevated goblet with a 3 s down and 3 s pause.
swaps.bodyweight: Pause squat with a 4 s descent and a 3 s pause, hands in prayer and elbows prying the knees, 15-20 reps.

cards.name: Romanian Deadlift
cards.doThisNotThat: Push your hips back to a wall behind you until the hamstrings are loaded, keeping a long spine. Don't bend at the waist and chase the floor with the bar.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism first: the hinge is the engine of sprinting and jumping. Lengthened hamstrings work also protects the streak.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop when the descent stops being controlled
prescription.tempo: 3 s down, 0 s pause, hips snap forward
prescription.slot: Main lift #2 on Legs day
prescription.warmup: 1 x 8 at ~50% with a 3 s descent

steps: Feet hip-width, bar or DBs in front of thighs, soft knees (~15-20° bend) that stay soft.
Tripod and screw the feet. Shoulders pulled down to the back pockets.
Push the hips straight back. The bar slides down the thighs, staying close.
Stop when the hips stop moving back (usually mid-shin). Then drive the hips forward.
cues: Hips reach back to touch the wall
Bar drags down your thighs
Push the floor away to stand

biomechanics.forceVector: Mostly horizontal at the hip: you swing the torso around the hip joint.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Knees fixed at ~15-20° flexion. Hip flexion ~70-90° at the bottom. Neutral spine throughout.
biomechanics.momentArm: The farther the bar drifts from your legs, the longer the lower-back moment arm. Keep it within 2-3 cm of the legs.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot tripod → fixed knee → hamstrings and glutes (hip extensors) → braced trunk → arms as hooks.
biomechanics.grf: Push down and slightly back through the heels and mid-foot. Too much weight on the toes means you're squatting it.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The bottom, where the hamstrings are longest and the hip moment arm is greatest.

neural.intent: Slow, controlled stretch on the way down, then a fast hip snap on the way up, like the start of a jump.
neural.rfd: Hip extension speed is the engine of sprinting and jumping. The snap teaches fast hip extension from a loaded stretch.

powerPair.exercise: DB or med-ball hip-hinge throw (or broad jump)
powerPair.rest: 20-30 s after each RDL set

cards.mobility: Loaded hamstring stretch in every rep. Your all-over stiffness includes the hamstrings, and loaded lengthening is a direct fix: you gain range you can actually control.
cards.footBase: Heavy RDLs tempt the feet to roll in. Keep the tripod, and screw the feet outward as you push the hips back; you'll feel the glutes engage and your balance improve.
cards.sequencing: Hips lead, torso follows. On the way up, the hips drive forward and the shoulders come along; don't pull with the lower back.

looks.effect: Hamstrings and glutes: the back of the legs, which fills out side profile and posture.
looks.lengthened: The hamstrings are loaded at long length at the bottom, the most growth-friendly part. Add 2-3 bottom-half partials after the last full rep.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Hip extension drives sprint acceleration and jump height, and loaded long-length hamstring work protects against hamstring strains in sprint sports.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Strong hinging builds the posterior chain for lifting and finishing takedowns, and a strong back line for clinch posture.

intensityTechnique.technique: 2-3 lengthened partials (bottom half only) after the last full rep

tips.tip: Finish the last set with bottom-half partials. Partials at long muscle length have trended as well as or better than full range in some studies, but recent trials show rough parity. Use them as an extra, not a replacement.
End the set when the descent stops being smooth or the back rounds, not when you can't lift it. Near-failure grows similarly to failure.
Use straps on heavy sets if grip limits you. Letting grip end the set means the hamstrings never got the stimulus.
Pair with Nordics in the week, not the same day at max volume. Both hammer the hamstrings eccentrically, and doing both hard on one day can leave you sore for sprinting and games.

cards.teachMe: Your hamstrings act like springs across the hip and knee. In sprinting they fight to stop your leg at the end of the swing, which is exactly when strains happen. The RDL teaches them to produce force while lengthening under control, so your nervous system lets you sprint at full speed without it pulling the handbrake.

swaps.home: Single-leg DB RDL, 3 s down, 6-10 per leg. One leg doubles the load on the hamstring with light DBs and trains the foot arch and balance too.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg RDL with a 4 s descent, reaching the opposite hand to the floor, 10-12 per leg. Add a slider hamstring curl after.

cards.name: Trap-Bar / Conventional Deadlift
cards.doThisNotThat: Use the trap bar and push the floor away like a jump, tight before the bar moves. Don't yank a conventional bar off the floor with a rounded back.
cards.priorityNote: Trap bar wins: it's more jump-like and safer for a growing spine, which beats the bigger conventional number.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop if the bar slows sharply or the back rounds
prescription.tempo: Controlled 2 s lowering, fast pull, reset each rep (no bouncing)
prescription.slot: Main lift #1 on a lower-power day (alternate weeks with squats)
prescription.warmup: 1 x 5 at ~50% moved as fast as possible

steps: Stand centred in the trap bar, feet hip-width. Tripod and screw the feet.
Hinge and squat down to grip the handles. Shins near-vertical, hips above knees, shoulders above the hips.
Pull the slack out of the bar (arms straight, lats tight) until it clicks, breathe and brace.
Push the floor away and stand tall. Lower with control.
cues: Push the floor away
Bend the bar handles toward your hips
Stand tall into the ceiling

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical. The trap bar keeps the load in line with your centre of mass, unlike the conventional bar which sits in front.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Start: knee flexion ~60-80°, hip flexion ~80-100°, trunk ~40-50° from vertical.
biomechanics.momentArm: The trap bar shortens the lower-back moment arm compared to conventional, so more work goes to legs and less to spine.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot tripod → knee and hip extension together → braced trunk transmits force → arms are hooks.
biomechanics.grf: Push straight down. Imagine leg-pressing the floor away. The bar rises because the earth pushes you up.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Off the floor, where the hip and knee moment arms are longest and nothing has momentum.

neural.intent: Every rep at maximum intended speed, even near-max weights. Pull the slack before you pull the bar.
neural.rfd: Taking the slack out first means force builds before the bar moves. That rapid tension rise is RFD — the same skill as exploding off the line.

powerPair.rest: 4-6 min after the last heavy set

cards.mobility: Hip-hinge positions under load grow the hamstring and hip range you can control. Lowering slowly through full range acts as loaded mobility.
cards.footBase: Heavy loads expose flat feet. Tripod and screw before you pull. If the arches cave as the bar leaves the floor, it's too heavy.
cards.sequencing: Knees and hips extend together. If the hips rise first, the back ends up doing the work.

looks.effect: Total posterior chain, traps, and grip: thicker upper back, glutes, and forearms.
looks.lengthened: Minimal lengthened stretch; this is a strength and power lift, not a growth driver. Get lengthened work from RDLs and split squats.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Trains whole-body force through triple extension (ankle, knee, hip), the same pattern as the jump and the sprint start.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Lifting from the floor with a braced spine is the pattern for picking up and finishing a double-leg takedown safely.

intensityTechnique.technique: None. No failure, no drop sets. Cluster sets (e.g., 2+2+2 with 15 s rest) if you want more quality reps.
intensityTechnique.when: Optional cluster on the last set

tips.tip: Stopping at ~20% velocity loss preserves explosive gains and costs less recovery than grinding (CMJ +9.5% vs +3.5% with 40% fewer reps).
Reset every rep. Touch-and-go reps use the bounce, so you don't train starting strength off the floor.
Use an external cue ('push the floor away') rather than 'squeeze the glutes'. External focus improves performance and learning.
Never heavy deadlifts within 48 h of a game. They tax the nervous system and back more than squats for the same effort.

cards.teachMe: Before the bar moves, your nervous system needs to know your body is locked tight. Taking the slack out tells it the joints are stable, so it fires harder. A loose start means your brain hesitates and the bar stalls off the floor.

swaps.home: DB suitcase or sumo DB deadlift with a 2 s pause just off the floor, 8-12 reps. Or single-leg DB RDL for heavier per-leg load.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg hip thrust (6 s hold at top) plus broad jumps for the power.

cards.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
cards.doThisNotThat: Lean the torso slightly forward and drop the back knee straight down, front foot screwed in. Don't stand bolt upright with a short stance and wobble side to side.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism wins: the single-leg version is the most sport-specific way to load your legs at home.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR
prescription.rest: 2 min between legs, 2.5 min between rounds
prescription.tempo: 3 s down, 1 s pause at the bottom, fast up
prescription.slot: Main lift #1 at home, or #2 on gym Legs day
prescription.warmup: 1 x 6 per leg bodyweight with a 2 s pause

steps: Back foot laces down on a bench or couch, ~2 shoe lengths in front.
Front foot: tripod and screw. Knee over the 2nd-3rd toe.
DBs in hands (or goblet). Slight forward lean from the hips (~15-20°).
Drop the back knee straight down to an inch above the floor, pause, drive up.
cues: Drop the back knee straight down
Push the floor away with the front foot
Stay level like a table

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical through the front foot. About 80-90% of the load goes through the front leg.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Front knee ~90-110° at the bottom; front hip ~90°; back hip in extension (stretching the hip flexor).
biomechanics.momentArm: More forward lean lengthens the hip moment arm (more glute). Upright with the knee forward shortens it (more quad).
biomechanics.kineticChain: Front foot tripod → knee → hip → pelvis held level by the glute medius → braced trunk.
biomechanics.grf: Push down through the front foot. Feel the pressure across the whole foot, not the inner edge where the flat foot collapses.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The bottom, where front-leg quads and glutes are longest and balance is hardest.

neural.intent: Controlled down; stand up explosively.
neural.rfd: Single-leg force with a stable pelvis is how sprinting, cutting, and punching actually load the leg.

powerPair.exercise: Split-stance jump switches or single-leg box jump
powerPair.rest: 20-30 s after each set

cards.mobility: Two at once: a deep front-leg hip/knee range and a loaded hip-flexor stretch on the back leg. Hip flexors are the main thing locked up in your stiffness pattern.
cards.footBase: Single-leg is where flat feet fail most visibly. Tripod and screw the front foot; if the knee dives in, the arch collapsed. Fix it: lighter load, slower descent, and big-toe ball pressing down.

looks.effect: Quads and glutes; balances leg size left to right.
looks.lengthened: The bottom range loads the glutes and quads at long lengths. Add 3-4 bottom-half partials after the last full rep.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Most athletic movement happens on one leg. Building single-leg force with a stable pelvis and arch transfers to cutting, sprinting, and stride efficiency.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Split stance is your fighting stance. Strong single-leg drive and a stable lead foot make your punches land with your weight behind them, and your penetration step stronger.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials (bottom half) to failure after the last full rep

tips.tip: Bottom-half partials after the last full rep add stimulus at long muscle lengths. Use them as a finisher, not a replacement.
Light DBs at home: slow the descent to 3 s and pause 1 s. Ending the set close to failure grows similar muscle across a wide range of loads.
Start with your weaker leg and match reps on the stronger leg. That evens out imbalances over time.

Too short a stance makes the front heel rise and stresses the knee. Too long a stance stretches the back hip flexor too far. Find the spot where the front shin is ~vertical at the bottom for glute bias.

cards.teachMe: On one leg your pelvis wants to drop on the unsupported side, and your arch wants to collapse. Your nervous system must coordinate the foot, knee, and hip at the same time. Training this teaches your brain to stabilize your leg automatically during sprints and cuts, so force goes into the ground instead of leaking sideways.

swaps.home: This is the best home leg exercise. Use the heaviest DBs, 3 s down, 1 s pause. If too easy, add a 1½ rep.
swaps.bodyweight: Bodyweight BSS 4 s down, 2 s pause, 12-20 per leg; or skater squats.

cards.name: Walking Lunge
cards.doThisNotThat: Land each step heel-to-tripod and pull yourself forward over the foot. Don't fall into each step on your toes with the knee collapsing in.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism: the deceleration and stability you build here is the main point, not the volume.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR
prescription.tempo: Controlled landing (stick 1 s), fast drive through
prescription.slot: Accessory after the main lift, or a conditioning finisher

steps: DBs at your sides, tall posture.
Step forward ~1 stride length. Land heel then whole foot; screw it in.
Drop the back knee toward the floor; front knee over the toes.
Drive through the front foot and pull into the next step.
cues: Land quiet, stick it
Push the floor behind you
Head stays level, no bobbing

biomechanics.forceVector: Mix of vertical and horizontal braking on landing, then horizontal propulsion.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Front knee ~90°, front hip ~90°, back knee near the floor.
biomechanics.momentArm: Longer step = more hip/glute; shorter step = more knee/quad.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Landing foot tripod → absorbing knee → hip → trunk stays stacked over the pelvis.
biomechanics.grf: On landing the ground pushes back hard; absorb it through the whole foot so the arch, not the knee, takes the impact.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The landing and the first push out of the bottom.

neural.intent: Soft, controlled landing; powerful drive.
neural.rfd: Deceleration control: how fast you can absorb force is the base for cutting and changing direction.

powerPair.rest: 20-30 s after each lunge set

cards.mobility: Each step stretches the back leg's hip flexor under load and takes the front hip through deep flexion. Moving mobility for a stiff body.
cards.footBase: Every step is a single-leg landing. Land and screw: tripod, rotate outward, arch up. Your knee won't cave if the arch holds.

looks.effect: Quads and glutes: legs that look athletic.
looks.lengthened: Use long steps and a deep bottom for glutes at long length.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Lunging is a sport pattern: reaching volleys, defensive slides, decelerating to cut. Strong, controlled lunges mean you can reach without losing balance.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Lunge mechanics are the penetration step for a double leg; a stable lead knee keeps you from overextending.

intensityTechnique.technique: Mechanical drop set: weighted lunges to near-failure, drop DBs, continue bodyweight
intensityTechnique.when: Last set (skip within 48 h of a game)

tips.tip: Stick the landing for 1 s. This installs balance — the 'Step-and-Stick' drill under load.
Reverse lunges are kinder on the knees and easier to balance; walking lunges add more deceleration. Use reverse if your knees ache.
Use an external focus ('push the floor behind you') for better performance and learning.

cards.teachMe: When you lunge, your brain predicts the impact and sets up stiffness in the leg before the foot lands. Practicing controlled landings teaches it to pre-tense the right muscles at the right time, which is why your balance gets better on the court.

swaps.home: DB reverse lunges from a 5-10 cm deficit (front foot on a step), 3 s down, 8-12 per leg.
swaps.bodyweight: Walking lunges with a 2 s pause at the bottom, or jumping lunges for power (3 x 6 per leg).

cards.name: Nordic Hamstring Curl
cards.doThisNotThat: Lower yourself as slowly as you can with hips extended, then catch with your hands and push back up. Don't bend at the hips to cheat the lowering.
cards.priorityNote: Injury-proofing protects the streak, which keeps the athleticism progressing.

prescription.load: Bodyweight; progress by lowering further before catching
prescription.tempo: 4-6 s lowering, catch with hands, push back up
prescription.slot: Accessory on Legs day, or 1-2x per week standalone

steps: Kneel on a pad. Anchor the heels under a couch, heavy DB, or a partner (sibling sits on your calves).
Body straight from knees to head, hips locked out, arms ready in front of the chest.
Lower forward as slowly as possible, keeping the hips extended.
Catch yourself in a push-up, push back up to the start.
cues: Fall like a tree
Shoulders stay in line with knees and hips
Push the heels into the anchor

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls your torso forward; the hamstrings brake the knee extension eccentrically.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hips fixed at 0° (extended); knee goes from 90° to as close to 0° as you can control.
biomechanics.momentArm: The moment arm grows as you fall forward, so the load climbs toward the bottom.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Anchored heel → knee joint → hamstrings → hips locked by the glutes → trunk straight.
biomechanics.grf: Here you push into the anchor, not the ground. The harder you drive the heels back, the more hamstring you recruit.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The final 30-45° before you catch, where the moment arm is longest.

neural.intent: Fight the floor every millimetre of the way down.
neural.rfd: Eccentric strength in the hamstrings is what stops your leg during the late swing of a sprint, when strains happen.

powerPair.exercise: None (don't pair power with a high-eccentric injury-prevention exercise)

cards.mobility: Eccentric loading at long length can increase the fascicle length of the hamstrings, which is linked to better range and resilience.
cards.footBase: Not standing, but the foot matters: point the toes into the floor and drive the heels up into the anchor to create tension through the whole posterior chain.

looks.effect: Hamstring size, especially in the lower part near the knee.
looks.lengthened: Heavy eccentric load with the knee extending: built-in long-length stimulus.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Protects against hamstring strains during max-speed sprinting and kicking.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Strong hamstrings help in the guard (BJJ heel hooks into the hips) and in powering through double legs.

intensityTechnique.technique: None. Pure eccentric quality.

tips.tip: Programs that include Nordics reduced hamstring injuries by up to ~51% (van Dyk 2019). A later reappraisal found the effect less certain, but it's still among the best-supported prevention tools.
Low volume works: 2-3 sets of 3-6, once or twice a week. You don't need more for protection.
Expect big soreness the first 2 sessions. Start with 2 x 3 and do them 3+ days before a game.
No eccentric-heavy work within 48 h of a game or fight. Nordics are the main one to skip.

cards.teachMe: At top speed your hamstrings act like brakes, slowing your lower leg before your foot strikes. If they can't produce enough force while lengthening, they tear. Nordics train exactly that: force while lengthening. Your nervous system learns the brake can handle the load, so it stops cutting your stride short.

swaps.home: This is a home exercise. Anchor under the couch or have your sibling hold your heels.
swaps.bodyweight: Same. Too hard: use a band-free assist by pushing off a chair seat; or do slider leg curls with a 4 s lowering.

cards.name: Standing Calf Raise
cards.doThisNotThat: Drop deep below the step with a 2 s stretch pause, then rise onto the big-toe ball. Don't bounce through the top half on the outside of the foot.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism and looks align: Achilles stiffness for sprint/jump, and calves for proportion.

prescription.load: Last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2 s down, 2 s pause in the stretch, 1 s up, 1 s squeeze
prescription.slot: Accessory/finisher on Legs day

steps: Ball of the foot on a step edge. Hold a wall with one hand, DB in the other.
Knee straight but not locked (gastrocnemius bias).
Lower until the heel is as low as it goes, pause 2 s.
Rise up onto the big-toe ball as high as possible.
cues: Push the step down with the big toe
Heel drops toward the floor
Grow tall at the top

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical through the ball of the foot.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Ankle dorsiflexion ~15-25° at the bottom to plantarflexion ~40-50° at the top.
biomechanics.momentArm: The foot is a lever: the ball of the foot is the pivot, the Achilles the force arm.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Big toe → arch → ankle → Achilles → calf muscles.
biomechanics.grf: Push down through the big-toe ball. Rolling to the outside (pinky toe) lets the arch collapse and weakens the push.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The stretched bottom, where the calf is longest.

neural.intent: Control the stretch, then push up hard.
neural.rfd: Fast ankle extension powers sprint push-off and jumps.

powerPair.rest: 20-30 s after each set

cards.elastic: Your Achilles is your spring. Heavy, slow calf loading increases its stiffness, so it stores and returns more energy each step. Pair with pogos to teach the spring to fire fast.
cards.mobility: The deep stretch pause at the bottom works ankle dorsiflexion, which limits your squat depth and running mechanics.
cards.footBase: Rise onto the big-toe ball and keep the arch lifted. That's short-foot work under load and directly trains the muscles that hold your arch up.

looks.effect: Calves: lower-leg proportion that matches your quads.
looks.lengthened: Partial reps in the bottom half grew the medial gastrocnemius more than top-half work (Kassiano 2023). Finish sets with bottom partials.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Achilles stiffness and calf strength drive sprint push-off and jumping, and lower the energy cost of running (economy) for XC.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Boxers live on the balls of their feet. Calf endurance and stiffness keep footwork bouncy through late rounds.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials to failure

tips.tip: Partials in the stretched (bottom) half grew the medial gastrocnemius more than full or top-half reps.
Straight knee targets the gastrocnemius; bent knee (seated) shifts to the soleus, which is critical for running.
Pause 2 s at the bottom to kill the bounce. Otherwise the Achilles does the work and the muscle doesn't.
Do them barefoot. The foot has to stabilize itself, which trains the arch.

cards.teachMe: Your Achilles stores elastic energy like a spring when it's stretched, then snaps it back. Heavy calf work stiffens the spring so it returns more energy with each step. That's why strong calves make sprinting and jumping feel free and why runners get more economical with strength work.

swaps.home: Single-leg calf raise on a stair with a DB, 2 s stretch pause, to failure.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg calf raise on a stair, 3 s down, 2 s pause; 15-25 reps to failure, then partials.

cards.name: Leg Press
cards.doThisNotThat: Go deep with the lower back pinned and feet screwed into the plate. Don't load the stack and do quarter reps with the hips peeling off the pad.
cards.priorityNote: Looks wins here: it's a hypertrophy tool that lets you train quads hard without the balance/back fatigue.

prescription.load: Last set to failure (it's a machine, safe to fail)
prescription.tempo: 3 s down, no pause, fast up (don't lock out hard)
prescription.slot: Accessory after squats or BSS

steps: Sit with the lower back flat on the pad.
Feet shoulder-width, middle of the plate. Lower placement = more quad; higher = more glute/hamstring.
Screw the feet into the plate (tripod down, rotate out).
Lower until the knees reach ~90° or just before the lower back lifts.
cues: Push the plate through the wall
Lower back stays glued to the pad
Knees track toward the pinky toes

biomechanics.forceVector: Along the line of the sled; fixed path, no balance needed.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Knee flexion ~90-110° at the bottom; hip flexion depends on seat angle.
biomechanics.momentArm: Lower foot position lengthens the knee moment arm (quad bias).
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot → knee → hip; trunk supported by the pad, so the legs are the limit.
biomechanics.grf: The plate is your ground. Push through the whole foot.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Deepest point, where the quads are lengthened.

neural.intent: Controlled down, powerful up.
neural.rfd: Lower RFD value than free weights since balance is removed, but good for building quad size.

cards.mobility: Deep knee and hip flexion with the back supported is a safe way to load full range.
cards.footBase: Even on a machine, screw the feet into the plate. It teaches the arch-up habit and keeps the knees aligned.

looks.effect: Quads, especially the outer and inner heads.
looks.lengthened: Spend time in the deep part. Lengthened partials in the bottom half after full reps.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Builds quad size and strength without balance demands; supports the free-weight lifts.

intensityTechnique.technique: Drop set: failure, drop 30%, failure again
intensityTechnique.when: Last set (not within 48 h of a game)

tips.tip: Failure on machines is lower risk. True failure on isolations and machines is fine; save the free weights for 1-2 RIR.
Bottom-half partials target the quads at long length, which may help growth.
If the lower back rounds off the pad, you've gone too deep for your hip mobility. Stop just before that point.

cards.teachMe: The leg press removes balance from the equation. Your nervous system doesn't need to stabilize, so it can send all its drive to the legs. Use it to build size; use squats and split squats to teach the body to use that size.

swaps.home: Heels-elevated DB goblet squat or BSS with a 3 s descent.
swaps.bodyweight: Sissy squat or heels-elevated slow squat, 15-25 reps.

cards.name: Pogo Hops
cards.doThisNotThat: Bounce off the floor like it's hot — stiff ankles, minimal knee bend, under 0.2 s contact. Don't do slow, deep jumps with soft knees.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism: elasticity and stiffness are what make you look and move fast.

prescription.load: Bodyweight
prescription.tempo: Fast as possible, minimal ground contact
prescription.slot: CNS prime or before runs

steps: Stand tall, feet hip-width. Tripod.
Lock the ankles slightly upward (toes pulled up toward shins).
Bounce off the balls of the feet with minimal knee bend.
Arms can swing small to help rhythm.
cues: The floor is hot
Bounce like a basketball
Quiet, quick contacts

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Knee flexion <20°; ankle near neutral on contact.
biomechanics.momentArm: The foot lever; the Achilles stores and releases the energy.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot → ankle stiffness → Achilles → calves; knee and hip stay stiff.
biomechanics.grf: Large, brief impact forces. Short contacts mean the force comes fast, which trains the tendon to be springy.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Contact: the faster you leave the ground, the better.

neural.intent: Stiff, fast, reactive.
neural.rfd: Reactive strength: how fast you turn landing into takeoff.

cards.elastic: The Achilles is a spring. On contact it stretches, storing energy; a stiff ankle snaps it back. Shorter ground contacts (<0.2 s) use the stretch-shortening cycle best.
cards.mobility: Low mobility demand. But fast ankle bounce teaches the joint to be stable and quick at the same time.
cards.footBase: Bounce off the big-toe ball with the arch up. If your arch collapses on each landing, cut the height and reps.

looks.effect: Minimal hypertrophy. This is an athleticism tool.
looks.lengthened: N/A.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Stiffer, faster ankles improve elastic return in sprinting and jumping, and lower the energy cost of running.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Light, bouncy footwork in boxing comes from reactive ankles. Pogos are the foundation.

intensityTechnique.technique: None. Quality over quantity.

tips.tip: Do them before runs. They prime the Achilles spring and make your stride bouncier.
Stop the set when contacts get loud or slow. Fatigue kills the elastic effect.
Heavy calf work plus plyos improves running economy.

cards.teachMe: When your foot hits the ground, the Achilles stretches and stores elastic energy. If your nervous system stiffens the ankle at the right time, that energy snaps back and pushes you up for free. Pogos teach your brain the timing of that spring. More spring means less muscle effort for the same speed.

swaps.home: Same, on any hard floor or outside.
swaps.bodyweight: Same.

cards.name: Broad Jump
cards.doThisNotThat: Load the hips, swing the arms back hard, then explode out at ~45° and stick the landing for 1 s. Don't jump without the arm swing and land stumbling.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism: horizontal power and landing control in one move.

prescription.load: Bodyweight
prescription.rest: 60-90 s between jumps, 2 min between sets
prescription.tempo: Max effort
prescription.slot: Power block or PAPE pair after squats/deadlifts

steps: Feet hip-width, tripod and screw.
Swing arms back while hinging the hips (like an RDL).
Explode forward: arms swing forward and up, hips extend.
Land feet hip-width, knees soft, stick for 1 s.
cues: Throw your hips to the far line
Arms reach for the horizon
Land quiet and freeze

biomechanics.forceVector: 45° forward and up.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hip hinge ~60-90°, knee ~90-110° at the loading position.
biomechanics.momentArm: Arm swing adds momentum; the hip hinge loads the glutes and hamstrings.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Arm swing → hip hinge → knee → ankle extension → takeoff.
biomechanics.grf: Push the ground down and back. The angle of push determines the angle of flight.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Transition from hinge to takeoff, and the landing.

neural.intent: Max intent every jump.
neural.rfd: Fast hip extension; the countermovement uses the stretch-shortening cycle.

cards.elastic: The quick countermovement (hinge then jump) stores elastic energy in the hamstrings, glutes, and Achilles. A fast, smooth reversal (not pausing) maximizes it.
cards.mobility: The hip hinge loads the hamstrings and glutes at length.
cards.footBase: Tripod on takeoff, and land in the tripod. If your knees collapse on landing, your arch did too. Shorten the jump until landing is clean.
cards.sequencing: Arms and hips work together. Arms swing back as the hips load, then swing forward as the hips extend. That synchronized whip adds real distance over a no-arm jump (grade B, jump biomechanics).

looks.effect: None directly. This is athleticism.
looks.lengthened: N/A.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Horizontal force production is the base of sprint acceleration and first-step quickness.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Horizontal hip drive is the penetration step on a double leg and blitzing forward in striking.

intensityTechnique.technique: None.

tips.tip: Track your best jump each week. It's one of your athleticism score tests; aim for small, steady PRs.
Doing 3 broad jumps 4-6 minutes after a heavy squat set can boost them (PAPE). Short rest (20-30 s) is contrast training, a different effect.
Stick every landing for 1 s. That's the Step-and-Stick drill: it installs landing control.

cards.teachMe: Jump distance is all about how fast you can push the ground. The faster you reverse from the hinge, the more elastic energy you use. The arm swing adds momentum and sets the timing. The landing teaches your brain to absorb force safely, so it lets you jump harder next time.

swaps.home: Same, outside or on a long hallway rug.
swaps.bodyweight: Same.

cards.name: Box Jump
cards.doThisNotThat: Jump as high as possible and land softly on a box at hip height or below, then step down. Don't jump onto a box so high you have to tuck your knees to your chest.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism: vertical power with a low landing impact.

prescription.load: Bodyweight
prescription.rest: 60 s between jumps, 2 min between sets
prescription.tempo: Max effort
prescription.slot: Power block or PAPE pair

steps: Stand 30 cm from the box, tripod and screw.
Swing arms back while hinging and bending the knees.
Explode up; arms drive up.
Land softly on the box in the same position you took off; step down.
cues: Jump to the ceiling
Land like a cat
Step down, never jump down

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Loading: hip ~60-90°, knee ~90°. Landing: knee ~90° (same as takeoff).
biomechanics.momentArm: Arm swing adds momentum.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Arm swing → hip → knee → ankle → takeoff.
biomechanics.grf: Push straight down. The box lowers the landing impact.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Takeoff.

neural.intent: Max intent jump; soft landing.
neural.rfd: Vertical power through fast triple extension.

cards.elastic: The countermovement uses the stretch-shortening cycle. A fast drop and reversal stores more elastic energy.
cards.mobility: Low demand.
cards.footBase: Take off and land in the tripod. Knees collapsing on the box means the arch collapsed. Keep the box low until landings are clean.
cards.sequencing: Arms and hips sync. Arms swing back as the hips load, then explode upward together.

looks.effect: None.
looks.lengthened: N/A.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Vertical power for rebounding, blocking, heading.

intensityTechnique.technique: None.

tips.tip: Step down from the box. Jumping down adds landing stress without benefit here.
The box measures your hip flexibility, not your jump. A higher box with a tucked landing doesn't mean you jumped higher.
Use an external focus ('jump to the ceiling') to boost performance.

cards.teachMe: A box jump lets you jump high without the hard landing. That means your nervous system feels safe and lets you jump all-out. Use it to practice max power with low risk.

swaps.home: Jump onto a sturdy step, couch edge, or just do vertical jumps with a soft landing.
swaps.bodyweight: Vertical jump with stick landing.

cards.name: Copenhagen Plank
cards.doThisNotThat: Top leg on a bench, body straight, push the bench down with the inner thigh. Don't sag the hips or bend the top knee to make it easy.
cards.priorityNote: Injury-proofing: groin health keeps you cutting, kicking, and sprawling.

prescription.load: Bodyweight
prescription.tempo: Hold or 2 s up, 2 s down
prescription.slot: Accessory on Legs day, or 1-3x per week standalone

steps: Side plank with the top leg on a bench (inner ankle/knee on top).
Bottom leg hangs or rests below.
Lift your hips so the body is straight. Hold or pulse.
cues: Push the bench down with your top leg
Hips stay high
Body straight like a board

biomechanics.forceVector: Lateral; the top adductor pulls you toward the bench.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hip neutral, knee straight (long lever) or bent (short lever).
biomechanics.momentArm: Long lever (ankle on bench) is much harder than short lever (knee on bench).
biomechanics.kineticChain: Top-leg adductors → pelvis → obliques → shoulder support.
biomechanics.grf: Push down into the bench; it pushes you up.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Holding the hips high.

neural.intent: Steady tension.
neural.rfd: Low; strength-endurance focus.

cards.mobility: Loads the adductors at moderate length.
cards.footBase: The bottom foot can push into the floor (if touching) for stability. Not a standing lift, but keep the top foot active.

looks.effect: Inner thigh and obliques.
looks.lengthened: N/A.
