sportTransfer.mechanism: Strong adductors protect against groin strains when cutting, kicking, and changing direction.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Adductor strength helps in the clinch, closing guard in BJJ, and squeezing in wrestling.

intensityTechnique.technique: None.

tips.tip: A Copenhagen-only program reduced groin problems in soccer players (odds ratio 0.59, about 41% lower odds).
Use the short lever (knee on bench) until you can hold 30 s with perfect form.
Low dose works. One exercise, 3x per week in preseason and 1x per week in season.

cards.teachMe: When you cut or kick, the groin muscles fire to control the leg. If they're weak, they tear. Copenhagens build strength in exactly that position. Your brain gets a stronger, safer muscle there, so it lets you cut harder.

swaps.home: Same: use a couch or chair.
swaps.bodyweight: Same.

cards.name: Overhead Dumbbell Triceps Extension
cards.doThisNotThat: Let the dumbbell sink until your hands touch your upper back and pause there 1 s, instead of bouncing at half depth: the bottom stretch is where the long head grows.
cards.priorityNote: Looks-driven lift; kept short (2-3 sets) so it never steals recovery from power work.

prescription.load: Sets 1-2 at 1-2 RIR; last set to failure, then lengthened partials
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s down, 1 s pause in the stretch, max-intent up
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day, after rows/pulls; first triceps exercise

steps: Sit on a bench or chair with back support, or stand in a split stance. Hold one dumbbell vertically with both palms under the top plate (diamond grip).
Press it overhead, upper arms beside your ears, elbows pointing at the ceiling (not flared past 20-30 deg).
Lower behind your head until the forearms pass parallel to the floor and the bell touches your upper back. Pause 1 s. Drive back to lockout.
cues: Point your elbows at the ceiling
Touch the bell to your upper back
Punch the dumbbell to the ceiling

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls straight down; the forearm rotates around the elbow, so resistance is the weight times the horizontal distance from elbow to bell.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder flexed ~170-180 deg (arm overhead) stretches the long head across two joints; elbow goes from ~40 deg to full extension.
biomechanics.momentArm: Moment arm peaks when forearm is horizontal (~90 deg elbow) and shrinks near lockout, so the bottom-to-middle range is the work zone.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Ribs down, glutes squeezed: a flared rib cage lets the lumbar spine arch and turns it into a back extension.
biomechanics.grf: Seated: minimal. Standing split stance: feet push the floor to stabilize the overhead load; no leg drive.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Coming out of the deep stretch, just as the forearm passes horizontal.

neural.intent: Control the stretch, then extend as fast as you can. Speed of intent recruits high-threshold units even on light loads.
neural.rfd: Low-RFD isolation; value is hypertrophy and elbow-tendon capacity for punching and throwing.

powerPair.dose: 1 x 4-5 before the first triceps set
powerPair.rest: ~4-6 min until the next heavy push

cards.mobility: Each rep loads the end range of shoulder flexion plus elbow flexion. That builds overhead ROM in a stiff thoracic spine/lats under control, which is what moves range: strength through full ROM roughly matches stretching for ROM (Afonso 2021).
cards.footBase: If standing: split stance, front foot screwed into the floor (rotate it outward without moving), tripod loaded. Seated: feet flat, same tripod pressure, so the brace starts from the ground.

looks.effect: Long head is ~the biggest triceps head and makes the back of the arm look full from the side and the back. More arm size than any curl.
looks.lengthened: The overhead position puts the long head at its longest length. On the last set, after failure, do 4-8 partials in the bottom half only (from stretch to forearm-horizontal).

sportTransfer.mechanism: Elbow extension finishes the punch, the overhead throw, the spike, and the jump-shot follow-through; tendon capacity at the elbow protects throwing volume.
sportTransfer.combatNote: The triceps snaps the jab and the cross out to full extension. A stronger long head helps you keep the guard up during long rounds.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials after failure
intensityTechnique.when: Last set: hit failure, then 4-8 bottom-half partials

tips.tip: Overhead arm position grew all three triceps heads more than the same extension done with arms at the sides; the long head grew most. That comparison was overhead vs neutral-arm extension, not pushdowns.
Overhead vs pushdown head-to-head: no significant difference, but the numbers leaned toward overhead. Use overhead as the default and pushdowns as the second movement.
Going to true failure adds little growth over stopping 1-3 reps short. Save failure for this last set, where the injury and fatigue cost is low.
If the elbows flare to ~45 deg, the lats and chest take over and the long-head stretch disappears. Use a lighter bell before letting the elbows drift.
Elbow aches? Switch to a single-arm version with a neutral wrist, cut the bottom 10 deg, and keep the stretch pause. Sharp joint-line pain means stop and swap.

cards.teachMe: A muscle that crosses two joints gets longest when both joints open it up. The long head crosses the shoulder AND the elbow, so raising the arm overhead pre-stretches it before the elbow even bends. Tension at long lengths is a strong growth signal. Your nervous system also only lets you load a range it trusts, so slow, controlled stretch reps teach it that the overhead position is safe. That's the threat-suppression idea, applied to a stiff shoulder.

swaps.home: Two-hand light-dumbbell overhead extension, seated on a chair: 3 x 15-20, 3 s lowering, 2 s pause in the stretch (light DB = more reps and more time at length).
swaps.bodyweight: Bodyweight triceps extension (sphinx-style or hands on a counter/table edge), lowering the forehead past the hands for the stretch: 3 x 8-15.

cards.name: Triceps Pushdown
cards.doThisNotThat: Lean forward ~15 deg with the elbows slightly in front of your ribs and let the hands rise to chin height on each rep, instead of chopping a half-range with elbows pinned behind your torso.
cards.priorityNote: Second triceps move; overhead extension takes priority for growth.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR on early sets; last set to failure + drop set
prescription.tempo: 2 s up (eccentric), max-intent down, 1 s squeeze at lockout
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day, after overhead extension

steps: Cable at top. Rope or bar. Step back half a step, staggered or split stance, hinge forward ~15 deg.
Elbows just in front of the ribs, upper arm angled slightly forward. Start with hands at chin height.
Push down to full lockout, spread the rope ends past your thighs, return under control to chin height.
cues: Spread the rope apart past your thighs
Push the handle toward the floor
Let the handle rise to your chin

biomechanics.forceVector: The cable pulls up and slightly back toward the pulley; the elbow extends against it.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder in slight flexion (~10-20 deg), elbow from ~30-40 deg flexion to full extension.
biomechanics.momentArm: Cable tension stays roughly constant through the range, so the resistance curve is flatter than a dumbbell's. Lockout still has load, unlike a skull crusher.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Brace, ribs down, hinge locked: if the torso pumps up and down, bodyweight is doing the rep.
biomechanics.grf: Feet press the floor to anchor the lean; the stance resists the cable pulling you toward the stack.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Final 20 deg to lockout (short-length peak contraction).

neural.intent: Drive down hard, resist the climb.
neural.rfd: Low; this is hypertrophy and elbow extension endurance work.

cards.mobility: Minimal range gain. Keep the high starting point (hands at chin) so the elbow works through near-full flexion.
cards.footBase: Split stance: front foot tripod (big-toe ball, pinky ball, heel) screwed outward so the arch rises and the knee tracks over toes; that keeps the lean stable without rocking.

looks.effect: Lateral head gives the horseshoe shape from the side.
looks.lengthened: Start each rep with hands at chin height so the elbow is ~30 deg flexed; on the last set finish with partials in the top half (hands chin to chest).

sportTransfer.mechanism: Lockout strength and elbow-extension endurance for repeated punches and blocks.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Builds triceps endurance for long rounds of punching, where the arm has to snap back to the guard each time.

intensityTechnique.technique: Drop set (-30% load, to failure)

tips.tip: Pushdowns trained the long head about the same as overhead extensions in the one direct trial, with numbers leaning overhead. Keep both in the week instead of choosing one.
Rope lets you spread apart at the bottom, for slightly more elbow extension and a stronger peak squeeze than a straight bar; use a V-bar if the wrists complain.
Taking the hands to chin height at the top adds roughly 30-40 deg of stretch per rep compared with the common 'chest-to-thigh' range, at zero cost.
A 90 s rest is enough for an isolation; save the 3-minute rests (Schoenfeld 2016) for compounds.

cards.teachMe: A cable keeps tension where a dumbbell drops it. At the bottom of a pushdown the cable still pulls the hand up, so the triceps works hardest when it's shortest. That's the opposite of the overhead extension, which loads the stretch. Training both ends of the length-tension curve covers the whole muscle. The nervous system learns lockouts as a unit, and that's the finish of every punch.

swaps.home: Single-arm dumbbell kickback with the torso hinged to parallel, from elbow fully bent to straight: 3 x 12-15, 1 s squeeze.
swaps.bodyweight: Bench/chair dips with feet on the floor (keep shoulders below ~60 deg extension) or diamond push-ups: 3 x 10-15.

cards.name: Close-Grip Push-Up
cards.doThisNotThat: Hands just inside shoulder width, elbows brushing the ribs at ~20-30 deg, lower until the chest touches your fists, instead of a diamond with elbows flared that grinds the wrists and shoulders.
cards.priorityNote: Home staple for triceps + pressing strength; adds power if done explosively.

prescription.sets: 3 working (1 warm-up set of 5 easy reps)
prescription.reps: 6-12 (add a backpack or raise feet when you get past 15)
prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop when rep speed visibly slows
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s down, explosive up
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day (home) or after the main press on Chest day
prescription.warmup: 1 x 5 at an easy incline (hands on a couch)

steps: Hands under the shoulders or slightly inside, index fingers forward, fingers spread and gripping the floor.
Body straight from heels to head: squeeze glutes, ribs down, eyes on a spot ~30 cm ahead of your hands.
Lower with elbows skimming the ribs until the chest touches the hands, then shove the floor away.
cues: Shove the floor away
Brush the elbows past the ribs
Chest to the fists

biomechanics.forceVector: You push the floor down and back; Newton's 3rd law sends your body up and slightly forward.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Elbow ~90-100 deg flexion at the bottom, shoulder ~20-30 deg abduction, wrists stacked under shoulders.
biomechanics.momentArm: Narrow hand placement puts the hands closer to the elbow line, increasing elbow flexion and triceps demand versus a wide push-up.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Plank tension (glutes, abs, serratus) transmits force from hands to feet; you move as one lever, so a sagging hip is a power leak.
biomechanics.grf: ~65-70% of bodyweight through the hands in a standard push-up; feet elevated raises it.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: First 5-8 cm off the floor, where elbow flexion is deepest.

neural.intent: Control down, launch up as fast as possible on every rep, even if the hands don't leave the floor.
neural.rfd: Explosive intent trains rate of force development in the push pattern; hands-off-floor is plyometric.

powerPair.exercise: Explosive push-up with hands leaving the floor
powerPair.rest: 30-45 s (contrast)

cards.elastic: Optional: drop into a catch and immediately bounce up (depth push-up from 5-10 cm risers) to train the stretch-shortening cycle in the chest/triceps.
cards.mobility: The full-depth chest-to-fist bottom opens the front of the shoulder and elbow flexion under load.

looks.effect: Triceps and inner/upper chest thickness; serratus definition if you push all the way through at the top.
looks.lengthened: Deficit: hands on two dumbbells or books so the chest sinks 5-8 cm below the hands for extra pec and triceps stretch.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Elbows-in pressing matches the straight-punch path and football hand strikes; the plank teaches the body to transmit force as one unit.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Elbows tight to ribs is the same path as a cross/straight punch: it protects the body and stops the force leaking out sideways.

intensityTechnique.technique: Rest-pause
intensityTechnique.when: Last set: to 1 RIR, rest 15 s, more reps to 1 RIR, x2

tips.tip: Low-load push-ups and bench press produced similar chest/triceps growth and strength gains when sets were taken close to failure; effort matters more than the implement.
Velocity loss: stop the set when the rep visibly slows. Grinding the last 20% of velocity costs power for little extra muscle.
Spread fingers and 'screw' the hands outward into the floor (right hand clockwise, left counter): the shoulders externally rotate and the elbows lock onto the ribs automatically.
Elevating the feet ~30 cm adds load and shifts it toward the upper chest and front delts; use it before adding a backpack.

cards.teachMe: A push-up is a moving plank. The floor pushes back exactly as hard as you push it, but force only gets to your body if every link between your hands and your feet is stiff. A loose core or sagging hips soak up force the way a flat tire soaks up a pothole. Tight elbows put the triceps and chest in a straight line behind the hand, which is the same thing you need to land a straight punch. Explosive intent on light reps teaches the motor cortex to recruit fast.

swaps.home: Feet-elevated close-grip push-up with hands on two dumbbells (deficit): 3 x 6-12.
swaps.bodyweight: Standard close-grip push-up, then incline (hands on a couch) to finish extra reps.

cards.name: Dumbbell Lateral Raise
cards.doThisNotThat: Lean ~15-20 deg toward the working side or hold a support, lead with the elbow to just above shoulder height, and move the dumbbell slightly in front of your body (scapular plane, ~30 deg forward), instead of swinging heavy bells straight out to the sides and shrugging.
cards.priorityNote: Top looks priority for the V-taper; low fatigue, so it fits on any day.

prescription.load: Light; 1-2 RIR sets 1-2; last set to failure + partials
prescription.tempo: 2 s up, 2-3 s down, no swing
prescription.slot: End of Chest+Bi or Back+Tri day; also good as the 'pump on demand' finisher

steps: Stand with a slight forward lean (hinge ~10 deg), dumbbells beside the thighs, elbows bent ~15-20 deg.
Raise the arms in a line ~30 deg in front of the frontal plane (scapular plane) until the upper arm is just above parallel.
Lower slowly to about 15 deg from the thigh; don't let the bell rest.
cues: Push the dumbbells out to the walls
Lead with the elbows
Keep the bells just in front of your thighs

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity acts straight down on a lever that rotates about the shoulder; you abduct the arm against it.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder abduction 0-~100 deg, elbow fixed at ~15-20 deg flexion, ~30 deg horizontal flexion (scapular plane).
biomechanics.momentArm: Zero at the bottom, maximal at 90 deg abduction. A dumbbell under-loads the bottom; leaning toward the working side or using a cable shifts tension lower.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Fixed torso, braced core. Any hip drive turns it into a front raise/swing and takes load off the delt.
biomechanics.grf: Feet stable on a tripod base; no leg contribution.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Top 20 deg, near horizontal.

neural.intent: Smooth and controlled; this is a hypertrophy isolation, not a power movement.
neural.rfd: Not relevant.

cards.mobility: Mild; the scapular-plane path keeps the shoulder out of impingement and trains upward rotation of the shoulder blade.
cards.footBase: Feet hip-width, tripod loaded, light screw outward so the arch is up and the knees are soft (~10-15 deg). A stable base stops the body rocking to cheat the weight up.

looks.effect: Wider shoulders, more of a V-taper (shoulder-to-waist ratio), the most visible look change per minute of work.
looks.lengthened: Do the last set leaning out ~20 deg (holding a doorframe) or single-arm cross-body so the delt is loaded from the bottom; finish with bottom-half partials (0-45 deg).

sportTransfer.mechanism: Shoulder endurance to hold the guard up, and supraspinatus/deltoid capacity for overhead sports.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Delts hold the guard; tired delts drop the hands. High-rep laterals build the endurance you need late in rounds.

intensityTechnique.technique: Mechanical drop set (strict reps to failure, then cheat-swing 5 reps controlling the negatives, then partials)

tips.tip: Light loads to near failure grow muscle about as well as heavy loads; for laterals, light and strict wins because heavy bells move the work to the traps.
The bottom 30 deg of a standing dumbbell raise has almost no resistance. A lean-away single-arm raise keeps the delt loaded in that range.
Pinky-up 'pouring' rotates the shoulder internally and pinches it. Keep the thumb slightly up or neutral.
Delts recover fast. 2-3 sessions a week of 3 sets fit easily within the 10-20 weekly hard-set target.

cards.teachMe: Shoulder width is mostly bone (the clavicle) plus the lateral delt sitting on top of it. You can't change the bone, but you can add thickness to the delt, which pushes the outline out and makes the waist look smaller by contrast. The trap tries to help on every heavy rep because the nervous system grabs the strongest available muscle. Light weight and an elbow-led path keep the lift on the target.

swaps.home: Light dumbbell lean-away single-arm lateral raise holding a doorframe: 3 x 15-25.
swaps.bodyweight: Side-lying lateral raise with a water bottle, or wall-slide 'Y' raises: 3 x 15-20.

cards.name: Dumbbell Overhead Press
cards.doThisNotThat: Press standing in a split stance with dumbbells on a slight forward path and the head moving 'through the window' at lockout, instead of seated and arching the low back with elbows flared straight out to the sides.
cards.priorityNote: Standing beats seated for athleticism; seated allowed if lower back is sore.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop when bar speed visibly slows
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s down, max-intent press
prescription.slot: Main press on an upper day, or second press after incline press

steps: Split stance (or feet hip-width), dumbbells at shoulder height, palms angled ~45 deg inward, elbows ~30 deg in front of the torso.
Squeeze glutes, ribs down. Press up and slightly in until the bells are over the middle of the foot, biceps by the ears.
Lower to the jaw/upper-chest line under control.
cues: Push the dumbbells through the ceiling
Head through the window at the top
Drive the floor away with the front foot

biomechanics.forceVector: Straight up against gravity; the bells should finish stacked over the shoulder joint and midfoot.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder from ~80-90 deg flexion/abduction to ~170 deg; elbow from ~70 deg to full extension.
biomechanics.momentArm: Largest at the bottom when the bells are furthest in front of the shoulder; scapular-plane path (~30 deg forward) reduces shoulder stress.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet -> glutes -> braced trunk -> scapula upward rotation (serratus/traps) -> humerus. A rib flare dumps force into the lumbar spine.
biomechanics.grf: Load + bodyweight goes straight down through the feet; the screw keeps the arch up and stops the knees caving.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Just above forehead height (sticking point).

neural.intent: Every rep as fast as possible concentric; cut the set when speed visibly drops.
neural.rfd: Moderate. The standing version trains force transfer from ground to overhead, like a block or a rebound.

powerPair.exercise: Dumbbell push press (dip-drive) or med-ball overhead throw
powerPair.rest: 4-6 min after a heavy set if PAPE; 30-60 s if contrast

cards.mobility: Full lockout trains overhead shoulder flexion and thoracic extension, two areas where a flat-foot posture cascade usually locks up (rounded upper back).
cards.footBase: Tripod both feet, screw the feet outward until the glutes switch on; in a split stance, drive the front foot through the big-toe ball. That is the base the press goes through.
cards.sequencing: Strict press: no hip drive. Push press: ground -> knee dip 10-15 cm -> hips/legs drive -> trunk transmits -> shoulders -> arms finish. Legs first, arms last.

looks.effect: Front and side delt mass, upper-chest tie-in, triceps.
looks.lengthened: Lower to jaw level with the elbows slightly in front for the delt stretch; last set finish with bottom-half partials.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Overhead force transfer for blocks, rebounds, stiff-arms and posting in wrestling; shoulder capacity for throwing.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Builds frame strength for the clinch and shoulder endurance to hold the guard; push press teaches legs-first force, like a punch.

intensityTechnique.technique: Negatives (push press up, 3-4 s strict lowering)
intensityTechnique.when: Last set, 2-3 reps after strict failure

tips.tip: Standing presses demand more trunk muscle activity than seated; choose standing when athleticism is the goal.
3-min rests produced more strength and leg growth than 1-min in trained men; give compounds the full rest.
A neutral/45 deg grip lowers the shoulder impingement risk vs palms forward and fits flat-foot posture (internally rotated shoulders).
If the low back arches at lockout, the overhead range is coming from the spine. Fix with half-kneeling presses until thoracic and lat range improves.

cards.teachMe: Pressing overhead standing is a test of your whole chain: if the feet collapse, the knees cave, the pelvis tips, the ribs flare and the shoulder loses its anchor. Force follows the path of least stiffness, so a leak anywhere bleeds into the press. Screwing the feet in and bracing builds a rigid column so the dumbbell rides on a solid tower. That's the same column you need when you take a hit or punch.

swaps.home: Half-kneeling single-arm light dumbbell press, 3-s eccentric, 3 x 10-15 each arm.
swaps.bodyweight: Pike push-up (feet on a chair for more load): 3 x 6-12.

cards.name: Face Pull
cards.doThisNotThat: Pull the rope to your eyes, then rotate your hands back so your knuckles point at the ceiling behind your head (double-biceps pose), instead of rowing to your chin with elbows down.
cards.priorityNote: Posture/shoulder health + looks; a cheap fix for flat-foot-driven rounded shoulders.

prescription.load: 1-3 RIR; never ugly reps
prescription.tempo: 1 s pull, 2 s hold at the back, 2 s return
prescription.slot: Warm-up for pressing days or finisher on Back + Triceps day

steps: Cable at forehead height or slightly higher, rope attachment, overhand thumbs-back grip.
Step back to tension, slight split stance, lean back ~5-10 deg.
Pull the rope apart toward your eyes, elbows high, rotate until fists are by your ears; return slowly.
cues: Pull the rope apart to your ears
Show the knuckles to the ceiling behind you
Finish in the double-biceps pose

biomechanics.forceVector: Horizontal-to-slightly-downward cable pull toward the face.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder horizontal abduction to ~0 deg (elbows in line with shoulders), external rotation ~70-90 deg at the end, elbow ~90 deg.
biomechanics.momentArm: Cable keeps constant tension; rear delts and external rotators are most loaded at end range.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet anchor -> core stops you being pulled forward -> scapulae retract and depress -> humerus externally rotates.
biomechanics.grf: Feet push forward against the floor to resist the cable.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: End position (full external rotation, elbows back).

neural.intent: Smooth; deliberate hold at the end.
neural.rfd: Not relevant; this is a positional/strength-endurance exercise.

cards.mobility: Builds shoulder external rotation under load, the end range a desk/phone/flat-foot posture loses first; better posture between sessions.
cards.footBase: Split stance, tripod on the front foot, rear heel down if you can; the screw keeps the arch up while you lean back.

looks.effect: Rear-delt cap for a 3-D shoulder, upper back thickness, and shoulders pulled back so the chest looks bigger.
looks.lengthened: Let the arms reach fully forward on each rep so the rear delts and rotators stretch; last set, partials in the front half.

sportTransfer.mechanism: External rotators decelerate the arm after punches, throws and serves; balancing all the pressing protects the shoulder.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Pulling the arm back to the guard after every punch is a rear delt job. Strong decelerators also let the nervous system 'allow' faster punches because it trusts the brakes.

intensityTechnique.technique: Long iso hold at end range (5 s) on final 3 reps

tips.tip: The nervous system caps speed based on how well it can decelerate a limb; building the brakes (rear delts and rotators) is a performance move, not just prehab.
Keep the elbows at or above wrist height: if the elbows drop, it becomes a row and the external rotation disappears.
Do 1-2 light sets before pressing as part of the warm-up; it adds weekly rear-delt volume at almost no recovery cost.

cards.teachMe: Your brain won't let you throw as hard as you could if it doesn't trust you can stop the arm safely. Every punch, throw and serve has to be braked, and the small muscles at the back of the shoulder do that. Training them is like putting better brakes on a car: you can drive faster because you can stop. It's also the strongest antidote to the rounded-forward posture flat feet push you into.

swaps.home: Prone (lying face-down on a bench or the floor) light-dumbbell 'Y-T-W' raises, 2-3 x 10 each letter.
swaps.bodyweight: Prone floor 'W' and 'Y' raises with 2-s holds, or doorframe reverse snow angels: 3 x 15.

cards.name: Neck Training
cards.doThisNotThat: Do slow, moderate-rep manual-resistance or light-plate neck work in all four directions (flexion, extension, left, right) 2-3x a week, instead of bridging or heavy jerky reps.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism (combat safety) first, looks second; never heavy or fast.

prescription.load: Light; 2-3 RIR. No failure, no jerking
prescription.tempo: 2 s each direction, 1 s hold at end range
prescription.slot: End of any session, or during the Fight Lab cooldown
prescription.warmup: 1 x 10 each direction unloaded through full range

steps: Flexion: lie on your back on a bench, head off the edge, hand or a folded towel with a light plate on the forehead; tuck the chin and curl the head up.
Extension: lie face down with head off the edge, resistance on the back of the head; raise the head to neutral, not past it.
Lateral: side-lying with head off the edge, or seated with your own hand pressing against the side of your head; move ear toward shoulder against resistance.
Manual: your sibling or your own hand gives smooth, even resistance through each direction.
cues: Nod the chin toward the ceiling (flexion)
Push the back of the head into the hand
Move the ear toward the shoulder smoothly

biomechanics.forceVector: Resistance against the head at varying angles; the cervical spine flexes/extends/laterally flexes around a stable base.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Flexion ~0-45 deg, extension back to neutral (avoid hyperextension under load), lateral flexion ~0-30 deg.
biomechanics.momentArm: Head-plus-load lever is short; small loads produce large torques at the cervical spine, so loads stay light.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Neck muscles connect head to the shoulder girdle; stiff neck + braced traps = one block absorbing a hit.
biomechanics.grf: Minimal; this is about absorbing external forces to the head.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: End range of each direction.

neural.intent: Smooth and controlled; build the reflex to brace, not speed.
neural.rfd: Low; the goal is stiffness and capacity, not speed.

cards.mobility: Full controlled cervical ROM under light load helps a neck that's stiff 'everywhere equally'; it trains the range instead of just stretching it.

looks.effect: Thicker neck that matches the shoulders and looks athletic; jawline appears sharper only through overall leanness and neck thickness, not structural jaw change.
looks.lengthened: Full range in each direction, with a pause at the stretched start position (e.g., head hanging back on flexion reps).

sportTransfer.mechanism: A stronger neck stiffens the head-neck system so impacts move the head less.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Every fighter trains neck: it helps you absorb punches and posture up under a front headlock or guillotine attempt. Never sparring-level contact with your sibling (levels 0-2).

intensityTechnique.technique: None (keep it submaximal)

tips.tip: Neck strength gains with progressive training are reliable; how much it reduces concussion risk is still debated, so treat it as useful insurance, not a shield.
Never train the neck heavy, fast or to failure; the cervical spine doesn't tolerate jerky loading. Add 1-2 reps per week, then add load.
Chin-tuck flexion (deep neck flexors) fixes forward head posture, which often goes with flat feet and rounded shoulders.
Stop on any tingling, numbness, headache or sharp pain and swap to isometrics against your hand.

cards.teachMe: Your head is a heavy ball on a thin stick. When it's hit, the ball accelerates, and the brain moves inside it. A stronger, stiffer neck ties the head to the torso so the hit gets spread over more mass, which means less acceleration (F = ma). The neck also protects your posture in grappling, where people try to pull your head down to break your stance.

swaps.home: Light dumbbell on a towel across the forehead (flexion) / back of the head (extension), lying on a bed or bench: 2 x 15-20 each.
swaps.bodyweight: Manual resistance with your own hand in 4 directions, 2 x 15 each, or 4-way isometric holds of 10 s.

cards.name: Farmer Carry
cards.doThisNotThat: Walk with short, quick steps, ribs stacked over pelvis, each foot landing on its tripod, instead of slow shuffles leaning back with the shoulders rolled forward.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism + functional strength; also a grip/forearm looks win.

prescription.load: Heaviest you can walk with good posture (aim toward bodyweight total over time); suitcase carry 1 DB
prescription.tempo: Quick, controlled steps
prescription.slot: Finisher on any lifting day or conditioning circuit

steps: Deadlift the dumbbells from the floor (hinge, flat back), stand tall.
Shoulders back and down, ribs down, look 5 m ahead.
Walk heel-to-toe with short steps; each foot rolls over its tripod. Turn by pivoting slowly.
cues: Crush the handles
Walk the floor back under you
Tall like a string pulls your head up

biomechanics.forceVector: Load pulls straight down through the shoulders; each stride sends ground reaction force up through a single leg.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Neutral spine, shoulders depressed and slightly retracted, hips fully extended between steps.
biomechanics.momentArm: Suitcase (one side) creates a lateral moment arm, so the obliques/QL of the opposite side fight lateral flexion.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot -> ankle -> knee -> hip -> trunk -> shoulder girdle -> grip, all stiffened while moving.
biomechanics.grf: Each step loads one leg with bodyweight + load; the foot arch has to hold under that.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Final 10 m when grip and posture fade.

neural.intent: Stay tall and quick, no leaning; grip as hard as possible.
neural.rfd: Low; teaches stiffness under load during locomotion.

cards.elastic: Quick short steps keep some ankle stiffness; avoid heavy stomping.
cards.mobility: Loaded upright posture with depressed shoulders reinforces thoracic extension and grounds the foot arch under load.
cards.footBase: Every step: land on a full tripod (heel, big-toe ball, pinky ball), screw the foot outward just enough to keep the arch up and the knee from caving. Barefoot or flat shoes at home build the short-foot strength best.
cards.sequencing: Locomotion pattern: foot plants, hip extends, opposite arm/shoulder stays stacked. Let the body move as one block from the ground up; don't let the shoulders swing ahead of the legs.

looks.effect: Forearms, traps and grip visibly; core tightness; posture.
looks.lengthened: Not lengthened-biased; for traps add a 2-s shrug pause at the end of each carry.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Grip endurance, trunk stiffness while moving, and single-leg stability.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Grip and trunk stiffness for clinching, controlling wrists, and keeping posture when someone hangs on you.

intensityTechnique.technique: Mixed carry (farmer 20 m -> suitcase 20 m each side)

tips.tip: Suitcase carries (one dumbbell) train anti-lateral-flexion: the core muscles opposite the weight do the work, a different stimulus to two-handed carries.
Carrying barefoot or in flat shoes is a time-efficient way to strengthen the intrinsic foot muscles alongside short-foot drills.
tips.source: grade B-C, foot intrinsic training literature

tips.tip: Grip fatigue cuts pulling performance; put carries at the end of a session, not before rows/pull-ups.
With light home dumbbells, slow the walk (3-s steps) or carry for time (60 s+) to make it hard.

cards.teachMe: A carry is a walking plank. Each step briefly puts the whole load on one leg, so the foot arch, knee, hip and trunk all have to stay stacked while you're moving. That's exactly what flat feet don't do automatically. You're training the foot to stay up when it's loaded, which is the base of all athletic movement. The grip work also fires up the shoulder stabilizers through a reflex called irradiation.

swaps.home: Light dumbbell suitcase carry for 60 s per side, slow controlled steps, or the heaviest bag you can carry around the house.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg balance walks (step-and-stick 1 s every step) with a 5-s single-leg hold every 5 steps, 3 x 30 m.

cards.name: Med-Ball Rotational Throw
cards.doThisNotThat: Load the BACK hip, then let the hips turn first and the arms come last like the end of a whip, instead of turning your shoulders and pushing the ball with your arms.
cards.priorityNote: Top athleticism priority: rotational power for every striking, throwing and racket sport.

prescription.load: 2-4 kg ball (light enough to be FAST); full rest between sets
prescription.rest: 60-90 s between sides; 2 min between sets
prescription.tempo: Max-intent explosive release
prescription.slot: After CNS prime, before main lifts or right after them as the power move
prescription.warmup: 5 easy throws each side at ~50% effort

steps: Stand side-on to a solid wall, ~1-2 m away, athletic stance (knees ~25 deg, hip hinge ~15 deg).
Ball at the back hip, weight on the back foot, chest over the back knee.
Drive the back foot into the ground, rotate the hips toward the wall, let the trunk follow, release the ball last with arms long. Catch off the bounce.
cues: Throw the ball through the wall
Turn the back knee toward the wall first
Let the ball be the last thing to move

biomechanics.forceVector: Horizontal rotational force; the ground is pushed backward and outward by the back foot, reacting forward and around.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Back hip internally rotates ~30-45 deg as you turn; trunk rotates ~60-90 deg; arms stay long but slightly flexed.
biomechanics.momentArm: Ball held at ~arm's length from the axis of rotation; longer arm = more ball speed for the same angular velocity (v = ωr), but harder to accelerate.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Ground -> back foot -> back hip -> pelvis -> trunk -> shoulders -> arms -> ball (proximal-to-distal).
biomechanics.grf: Back foot pushes into the ground first (horizontal shear), then the front leg blocks to transfer momentum up.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The switch from back-hip load to rotation; that's where the timing usually fails.

neural.intent: Maximum speed every rep; if a throw feels slower, stop the set.
neural.rfd: High-RFD rotational power; trains fast-twitch recruitment and intermuscular timing.

powerPair.exercise: Pair with a heavy split squat or row as contrast
powerPair.rest: ~4 min after the heavy set if you want potentiation; 30-60 s if contrast

cards.elastic: The loading 'wind-up' stretches the obliques and hip rotators; a quick countermovement into the throw uses the stretch-shortening cycle. Keep the switch quick (<0.3 s).
cards.mobility: Builds rotational range in the hips and thoracic spine under speed, where Jonah's all-over stiffness makes him rotate from the lower back instead.
cards.footBase: Back foot screws into the floor (rotating it outward without moving) to load the back glute; front foot lands on its tripod and 'blocks' so momentum flows up. A collapsed arch on the back foot leaks the force into the floor.
cards.sequencing: Ground -> back hip -> pelvis rotates first -> trunk follows ~50-80 ms later -> shoulders -> arms -> ball. The hips lead; the arms are just the whip's tip. If your arms move first, the throw is weak and random, the same fault as reaching for a ball in pickleball/tennis.

looks.effect: Athletic obliques and a tight, functional midsection.
looks.lengthened: Not a looks lift; the loaded wind-up does bias the obliques at length.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Same proximal-to-distal sequence as a punch, a bat swing, a forehand/backhand, a throw and a spike.
sportTransfer.combatNote: The hook and cross are rotational throws without a ball. Rotational medicine-ball throw speed relates to punching force (grade C).

intensityTechnique.technique: None (power work, never to fatigue)

tips.tip: Rotational med-ball throw velocity correlates with punch force; the punch is a ground-to-fist chain. Correlation, not proof of transfer.
Use the lightest ball that still challenges you (2-4 kg). Heavy balls slow the movement and turn power training into strength-endurance.
External cues ('throw through the wall') produce faster, more powerful throws than internal cues ('rotate your hips').
Both sides every session, but start with your weaker side when you're freshest.
Stop the set when the throw slows. Like velocity-loss training, fatigue just teaches slow movement.

cards.teachMe: Your power comes from the ground, not your arms. Each segment (hip, trunk, shoulder, arm) speeds up and then brakes, and passes its momentum to the next one, like cracking a whip. That's why the tip moves so fast. If the arms go first, there's nothing behind them, which is your backwards sequencing problem. The ball gives you instant feedback: a good throw is loud and feels effortless.

swaps.home: Dumbbell rotational punch-throw: hold a light dumbbell at the back hip with both hands, rotate explosively and 'punch' it forward to full arm extension (DON'T release), 3 x 5 each side. Or throw a heavy pillow/rolled blanket against a wall.
swaps.bodyweight: Hip snap drill: athletic stance, back hip loaded, snap the hips to face forward with arms loose and trailing, 3 x 8 each side; then rotational broad jumps 3 x 3 each side.

cards.name: Shadowboxing
cards.doThisNotThat: Shadowbox with intent at ~70% effort on a specific theme each round (e.g., jab + step), seeing an opponent in front of you, instead of flailing random combos at full speed.
cards.priorityNote: Boxing/MMA is the main love; skill work comes first, conditioning second. Contact ladder level 0.

prescription.load: ~70% effort (Zahabi); last round 85-90% as a 'finisher'
prescription.tempo: Rhythm + bursts: 2-3 s of fast combinations every ~10 s, then reset
prescription.slot: Warm-up before Fight Lab, standalone skill session, or the conditioning block on any day
prescription.warmup: 1 round at 50%: footwork only (stance, step-drag, pivots)

steps: Stance: feet a bit wider than shoulder width, lead toe and rear heel on a line slightly offset, weight 50/50, knees soft ~25 deg, chin down, hands at cheekbones.
Round themes in order of the striking progression: R1 stance/guard + footwork, R2 jab, R3 cross, R4 lead hook, R5 defense (parry/slip) after each combo, R6 combos (1-2, 1-2-3, slip-2).
Return to guard after every punch; exhale sharply on each strike.
cues: Hit the target 10 cm behind the opponent's chin
Bring your hand back to your cheek
Turn the back heel like crushing a bug

biomechanics.forceVector: Punch force starts as a horizontal push of the feet against the ground and leaves the fist as a straight-line projectile (jab/cross) or horizontal arc (hook).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Cross: rear foot pivots ~45-90 deg, hip rotates ~45 deg, trunk ~45 deg further, shoulder turns to cover the chin, elbow extends to ~170 deg (never locked). Lead hook: elbow ~90 deg, forearm parallel to floor.
biomechanics.momentArm: Straight punches use a short lever (fast); hooks use a longer lever from the rotating trunk (more momentum, slower).
biomechanics.kineticChain: Foot -> knee -> hip -> torso -> shoulder -> elbow -> fist.
biomechanics.grf: Rear foot drives horizontally into the floor on the cross; the lead leg blocks to stop the body moving forward and convert momentum to rotation.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Keeping the opposite hand on the chin at full extension, and resetting the stance after combinations.

neural.intent: Relaxed and fast. Tension only at impact (snap), then back to loose.
neural.rfd: Very high RFD per punch; relax-contract-relax cycle trains fast muscle switching.

powerPair.exercise: Med-ball rotational throws or plyo push-ups before rounds
powerPair.rest: 2-3 min, then shadowbox

cards.elastic: Bouncy stance (on the balls of the feet) keeps the Achilles springs loaded so you can move in and out quickly.
cards.mobility: Rotation through the hips and thoracic spine on every punch, plus slips and rolls (lateral flexion and squat-level changes), rehearsed at speed; it trains range where you're stiffest.
cards.footBase: In stance, the screw cue on both feet (rotate them outward without moving) keeps the arches up and knees soft. On every cross, the rear foot pivots on the ball of the foot, not the heel.
cards.sequencing: Hips lead, arm whips: ground -> hip -> trunk -> shoulder -> arm -> fist. Punches start in the feet. Your 'arm first' habit means the fist arrives before the body's mass is behind it, so the punch has no weight. Install the order: feel the rear foot push, the hip turn, THEN the arm extends as the last link.

looks.effect: Lean, conditioned look; shoulder and core endurance.
looks.lengthened: N/A (skill/conditioning).

sportTransfer.mechanism: Footwork, rotational sequencing, hand-eye timing, and conditioning that carries over to any reactive sport.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Contact ladder level 0 (no contact). Topuria-style: shadowbox daily, rotating emphasis blocks (striking-heavy weeks / grappling-heavy weeks). Zahabi: frequent rounds at ~70% beat rare all-out rounds. Danaher: go deep on 4-6 combos you'll actually use.

intensityTechnique.technique: Last-round finisher: 30 s straight punches (fast, light), 10 s rest x 3

tips.tip: Visualize a specific opponent's head and body moving. Imagery-based training engages the same motor networks as real fighting and makes rounds more transferable.
External focus ('hit through the target') beats internal ('extend your elbow') for both speed and learning.
Exhale sharply ('tss') on each punch: this braces the trunk and keeps you from breath-holding, important with EIB.
Use light 0.5-1 kg dumbbells only in slow technical rounds, never at speed; the extra weight changes timing and stresses the elbow at full extension.
Film one round a week from the side: check that the rear heel turns before the fist arrives.

cards.teachMe: Your nervous system learns what you repeat, and shadowboxing is pure repetition with no fear of getting hit. That matters: with no threat, the brain lets you relax, and relaxed muscles move faster. You're installing the order (feet, hips, trunk, arm) at 70% so that when the speed and stress go up, the pattern holds. Seeing an imaginary opponent also trains your eyes to lead the movement.

swaps.home: Same drill in any room; use a mirror or your phone camera for feedback. With sibling: pad work at contact ladder level 1 (pads/mitts) only.
swaps.bodyweight: Footwork ladder (step-drag, pivot, in-out) for 2-min rounds, plus slip-squat drill with a string across a doorway.

cards.name: Dead Bug
cards.doThisNotThat: Keep your low back glued to the floor and exhale fully as the opposite arm and leg reach out slowly, instead of flailing limbs while your back arches off the ground.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism: teaches the trunk to stay stiff while the limbs move, the base of sequencing.

prescription.load: Bodyweight; add a light dumbbell held overhead or a 3-5 s hold at full reach as it gets easy
prescription.tempo: 3 s reach, 1 s pause, 2 s return; full exhale on every reach
prescription.slot: CNS prime / warm-up before lifts, or core finisher

steps: Lie on your back, arms straight up toward the ceiling, hips and knees at 90 deg.
Exhale fully until your ribs drop and your lower back presses into the floor.
Slowly reach one arm overhead and the opposite leg out straight, hovering 5-10 cm off the floor; return and switch.
cues: Push your low back into the floor
Reach the heel to the far wall
Blow out all the air like a balloon

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity on the extended leg and arm creates a torque that tries to arch the lumbar spine (anti-extension).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hips extend from 90 deg to ~170 deg, shoulder flexes 90 to 180 deg, spine neutral-to-slightly flexed.
biomechanics.momentArm: Longest when the leg is straight and low; bending the knee shortens it (easier version).
biomechanics.kineticChain: Core stiffness keeps the pelvis still while the limbs move; it's the 'stable center, moving limbs' principle of every sport.
biomechanics.grf: Lumbar spine presses into the floor; the floor is your feedback.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Full reach with the leg 5-10 cm off the floor.

neural.intent: Slow and controlled; the drill is trunk stiffness, not speed.
neural.rfd: Not relevant.

cards.mobility: Teaches shoulder flexion and hip extension without the lumbar spine taking over, which is how stiff athletes 'fake' range.
cards.sequencing: Contralateral pattern (opposite arm and leg) is the same cross-body linkage as running, punching and throwing: the trunk is the anchor that lets opposite limbs work together.

looks.effect: Flat, tight midsection by improving deep-core control (a smaller-looking waist when you stand braced).
looks.lengthened: Add the overhead reach with a light dumbbell for a stretched-position rectus abdominis load.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Trunk stays stiff while the limbs move fast and in opposition, the basis of punching, sprinting and cutting.
sportTransfer.combatNote: A stiff trunk on every punch means force isn't lost in the midsection, and body shots hurt less when the core is braced on the exhale.

intensityTechnique.technique: Long isometric hold at full reach (5-10 s) on the last 2 reps each side

tips.tip: The full exhale is the key detail: it pulls the ribs down and sets the deep core; without it, it's just limb waving.
If the back lifts off the floor, shorten the lever (bend the knee) rather than speed up.
Pair with 90/90 breathing as a downshift drill before sessions; a calmer nervous system releases range.

cards.teachMe: Your arms and legs can only be as fast and powerful as the platform they attach to. If the middle bends every time a limb moves, force leaks out of the chain. The dead bug trains your trunk to stay a solid block while your opposite arm and leg move, which is exactly what has to happen in a punch or a sprint stride. The exhale tells your nervous system to brace, and it also downshifts out of the threat state.

swaps.home: Dead bug holding a light dumbbell in both hands overhead (arms only move), 3 x 8 slow leg reaches each side.
swaps.bodyweight: Standard dead bug; regress to bent-knee heel taps if the back lifts.

cards.name: Hip Thrust
cards.doThisNotThat: Tuck your chin, keep your ribs down and finish with a posterior pelvic tilt (hips under, not back arched), instead of hyperextending the lower back to push the hips higher.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism (hip extension for sprinting/jumping/punching) and looks.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR
prescription.tempo: Explode up, 1-2 s hold at top, 2 s down
prescription.slot: Legs day, after squats/RDLs

steps: Upper back on a bench edge (bottom of shoulder blades), barbell or dumbbell in the hip crease with a pad.
Feet flat, shins vertical at the top position, feet ~hip-width.
Drive through heels to full hip extension, chin tucked, ribs down; lower until the hips are ~10 cm off the floor.
cues: Drive the floor away with your heels
Push the bar to the ceiling
Keep your eyes on the wall in front

biomechanics.forceVector: Horizontal (anteroposterior) force relative to your body, the same direction as the propulsive push in sprint acceleration.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Hips from ~90 deg flexion to 0 deg (full extension), knees ~90 deg at lockout.
biomechanics.momentArm: Greatest at full hip extension (the load is furthest behind the hip axis), so glutes work hardest at their shortest.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet -> knees -> hips; the upper back on the bench is the pivot.
biomechanics.grf: Heels push down and slightly forward; the screw cue stops the knees caving.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Lockout (top 15 deg of hip extension).

neural.intent: Explosive hip extension each rep; control the descent.
neural.rfd: Moderate; trains the glute to contract hard at full hip extension, the finish of a sprint push-off.

powerPair.exercise: Broad jump or sprint start (3-5 s)
powerPair.rest: 4-6 min if PAPE; 30-60 s if contrast

cards.mobility: Full hip extension under load opens the front of the hip (hip flexors), which is often tight with a flat-foot posture and anterior pelvic tilt.
cards.footBase: Feet flat, screw them into the floor (rotate outward without moving) to fire glutes and keep knees out over the 2nd-3rd toes; press through the tripod so the arch stays up.

looks.effect: Glute size and shape; better posture and pelvis position.
looks.lengthened: Glutes are short at the top; add deep-range work elsewhere (RDLs, Bulgarian split squats) for the lengthened stimulus. Hip thrusts are the short-range complement.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Hip extension powers acceleration, jumping and rotation; strong glutes stabilize the knee against valgus.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Hip drive is what puts weight behind a punch and powers wrestling bridges and shots.

intensityTechnique.technique: Rest-pause or 3-s top holds on the final reps

tips.tip: Hip thrusts grew the glutes similarly to squats in a 2023 RCT, but squats also grew the quads and adductors. Use hip thrusts as an add-on, not a replacement.
Hip thrust training improved horizontal force in some studies, but its transfer to sprint speed is inconsistent; treat it as supportive, not the main speed driver.
Chin tucked keeps the ribs down and prevents lumbar extension from 'faking' the lockout.
Single-leg version with light dumbbells is a strong home option and adds a hip stability challenge.

cards.teachMe: Your glutes are the biggest muscle in your body and the main engine of hip extension: sprinting, jumping and putting your hips into a punch. Flat feet make the knees cave and the glutes switch off because the hip rotates in. Screwing your feet outward turns them back on. The hip thrust loads the glutes hardest at full extension, which is the exact position where you push off in sprinting.

swaps.home: Single-leg hip thrust on a couch with a light dumbbell on the hip, 3 x 10-15 each, 2-s hold at top.
swaps.bodyweight: Single-leg glute bridge or shoulders-elevated single-leg hip thrust, 3 x 12-20 each.

cards.name: Incline Dumbbell Press
cards.doThisNotThat: Set the bench at 30°, not 45°+ — past ~45° the front delt takes over and your upper chest loses the job.
cards.priorityNote: Looks (upper chest for the V-taper) leads here, but every rep is pressed with max intent so it still feeds punching power.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop the set when rep speed visibly slows
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s controlled lower, 1 s soft pause at the stretch, explode up
prescription.slot: Chest + Biceps day, first main lift after CNS prime
prescription.warmup: 1 set x 8 at ~50% of working weight, same tempo

steps: Bench at 30° (2nd or 3rd notch on most benches).
Kick the dumbbells up off your knees as you lie back — one at a time.
Shoulder blades pinched down and back like they're in your back pockets; small natural arch, butt stays on the bench.
Feet flat and slightly behind the knees; screw them into the floor.
Dumbbells start over your upper chest, forearms vertical, elbows ~45-60° from your torso (not flared to 90°).
cues: Push yourself away from the dumbbells into the bench.
Drive the floor away with your feet before each rep.
Bring the dumbbells down to the edges of your chest, then punch them to the ceiling.

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls straight down; at 30° incline the press path is aimed at the clavicular fibers' line of pull (shoulder flexion + horizontal adduction).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Bench 30°; upper arm ~45-60° from torso at the bottom; forearms vertical over the wrist the whole rep.
biomechanics.momentArm: Longest shoulder moment arm at the bottom when the elbows are deepest; forearm vertical keeps the elbow moment arm near zero so the chest and delt, not the triceps, own the bottom.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet → glutes → braced trunk → scapulae pinned → humerus → dumbbell. A pinned scapula is the stable base the pec pulls from; if it shrugs, force leaks.
biomechanics.grf: Leg drive creates a horizontal ground reaction force that pins your upper back into the bench, stiffening the base you press off (Newton's 3rd law).
biomechanics.hardestPoint: First 5-8 cm off the chest — longest moment arm, most stretch, least mechanical advantage.

neural.intent: Control down 2-3 s, then try to throw the dumbbells through the ceiling on every rep, even when they move slowly.
neural.rfd: Max-intent concentric trains rate of force development — the speed you reach high force, which is what a punch actually uses.

powerPair.exercise: Plyometric push-up (hands leave the floor) or med-ball chest pass into a wall
powerPair.rest: Do it ~4-6 min after your top set, then 90 s between power sets

cards.elastic: The 1 s pause at the bottom kills the bounce on working sets so the chest does the work; on the power pairing you do the opposite — fast stretch-shortening cycle.
cards.mobility: Every rep is a loaded stretch of the pecs and front delts at the bottom; with your all-over stiffness this builds usable shoulder extension range — loaded full-ROM work improves ROM about as well as stretching (Afonso 2021).
cards.footBase: Tripod foot (big-toe ball, pinky-toe ball, heel) flat on the floor, then screw both feet outward without moving them — glutes fire, knees stop caving, and your flat-foot arches stop collapsing into the drive.
cards.sequencing: Feet drive first, then the press — legs → trunk → arms. Same ground-up order as a cross; never let the arms start alone.

looks.effect: Upper chest fills the gap under the collarbone — the shelf that makes the chest look full in a T-shirt and widens the V-taper visually.
looks.lengthened: Get the dumbbells slightly below chest level with the upper arm just past the torso line at the bottom; that stretched position is where most of the growth stimulus sits. On the last set add 3-5 bottom-half partials.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Upward-angled horizontal pushing force: stiff-arm and blocking in football, finishing through contact in basketball, and the upper-chest/front-delt contribution to an uppercut or a cross thrown at a taller opponent.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Upper chest + front delt are part of the end of the punch chain. The press builds the force capacity; the plyo push-up teaches you to release it fast.

intensityTechnique.technique: Rest-pause: hit 1 RIR, rack on knees 15 s, 2-3 more reps; then 3-5 lengthened partials

tips.tip: Rest the full 2.5-3 min. Rushing to 1 min cuts reps and growth on compounds.
Stop 1-2 reps short; true failure on a heavy dumbbell press costs power and buys almost no extra growth.
Turn the dumbbells to a ~30° angle (pinky slightly in) instead of a straight barbell line — shoulders sit in a safer groove and you can press heavier.
Keep elbows under the wrists at the bottom — when the elbow drifts outside the wrist, the triceps take the load and the chest stimulus drops.
When you can do 10 clean reps on every set, go up to the next dumbbell — even if it's a big jump with light home dumbbells, drop back to 6 reps and climb again.

cards.teachMe: Your nervous system only lets you push as hard as your base feels stable. Pin the shoulder blades and drive the floor and the brain senses a solid platform, so it releases more motor units into the pec. Physics: force has to go through something stiff to move a load, so a loose base means leaked force and a weaker press. The 30° angle just lines up the force direction with the upper-chest fibers.

swaps.home: Floor-to-couch incline: hips on the floor, upper back on a couch cushion wedge, light DBs at slow 3-s lowers + 1-s pause, 12-20 reps to near failure.
swaps.bodyweight: Feet-elevated push-up (feet on a chair, ~30-45° decline body angle = incline press angle), hands slightly wider than shoulders, 8-20 reps.

studies: Afonso 2021 (strength training vs stretching for ROM)

cards.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
cards.doThisNotThat: Let the dumbbells sink a few cm below chest level each rep — don't stop where a barbell would; that extra stretch is the whole reason to use dumbbells.
cards.priorityNote: Looks + strength; kept as the second press so the incline (higher-priority upper chest) gets your freshest sets.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lower, 1 s pause at the stretch, explode up
prescription.slot: Chest + Biceps day, second press

steps: Flat bench, dumbbells kicked up off the knees.
Shoulder blades pinched down and back; keep the arch small and your butt on the bench.
Feet flat, slightly behind the knees, screwed into the floor.
Elbows ~45-60° from the torso; forearms vertical.
cues: Bend the handles into a 'V' as you press.
Push the floor away with your feet.
Punch the dumbbells up and together, stopping just before they touch.

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical press against gravity; the arm path is horizontal adduction + shoulder flexion — the sternal pec fibers' main line of pull.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Upper arm 45-60° from the torso; elbow ~90° at the bottom; wrists stacked over the elbows.
biomechanics.momentArm: The shoulder moment arm peaks at the bottom when the elbows are deepest; freedom of the dumbbells lets each arm find its strongest path.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Floor → legs → glutes → braced trunk → pinned scapulae → humerus → dumbbell.
biomechanics.grf: Pushing the floor horizontally pins your upper back into the bench — that's your stable anchor.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Bottom third, where the dumbbells are deepest and the pec is most stretched.

neural.intent: Controlled lowering, max-intent press. Each arm has to stabilize its own dumbbell — extra coordination demand that wakes up the shoulder stabilizers.
neural.rfd: Exploding off the pause trains starting strength — force from a dead stop, like throwing a punch from a set guard.

powerPair.exercise: Med-ball chest pass into a wall (or explosive clap push-up)
powerPair.rest: ~4-6 min after the top press set

cards.mobility: The dumbbells let you go deeper than a barbell, so every rep loads the pec and anterior shoulder at a longer length — expands your horizontal-abduction range under control.
cards.footBase: Tripod foot planted, screw outward — this is what gives you a real leg drive and stops your flat-foot arch from collapsing into a weak, wobbly base.
cards.sequencing: Legs drive → trunk braces → arms press. Feet move first, every rep.

looks.effect: Thickens the mid and lower chest so the pecs look full from the front, not just the top.
looks.lengthened: Hold 1 s at the bottom with the dumbbells just below chest level and the upper arms slightly past the torso line; on the last set add 3-5 bottom-half partials.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Horizontal push strength: framing and creating space from bottom position in BJJ, hand fighting and posting in wrestling, blocking in football.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Builds the push base for the cross and for framing off an opponent on your back. The pause rep mimics pushing from a dead stop.

intensityTechnique.technique: Drop set: at 1 RIR drop ~30% weight and go to 1 RIR again

tips.tip: Rep duration from 0.5-8 s grows muscle similarly — so lower under control, but don't waste effort on super-slow reps. Intent on the way up matters more.
If one arm reaches failure first, end the set there — grinding the weak side with a twisted torso just teaches asymmetry.
Don't clang the dumbbells together at the top — stop ~5 cm apart; tension stays on the chest and the lockout doesn't turn into a rest.
Two to three hard sets of near-failure training here is plenty for growth; extra failure sets cut into recovery for your sport and gain little.

cards.teachMe: Two separate dumbbells force each shoulder to stabilize itself — the rotator cuff and serratus have to fire in order, which trains the stability your shoulder needs to punch hard without leaking force. The deeper bottom also stretches the pec more under load, and muscles under tension at long lengths are a strong growth signal.

swaps.home: Floor press with light DBs: elbows touch the floor, 1-s pause, then explode up; 12-20 reps to near failure.
swaps.bodyweight: Deficit push-up between two chairs or stacks of books, chest below hand level, 8-20 reps.

cards.name: Barbell Bench Press
cards.doThisNotThat: Touch the bar to your lower chest/sternum with elbows ~45-60° tucked — not to your neck with elbows flared to 90°.
cards.priorityNote: Functional strength + looks. Kept to 4-6 reps at 1-2 RIR so it doesn't eat power for sport.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; true failure only with safeties set or a spotter
prescription.tempo: 2 s lower, touch, explode
prescription.slot: Chest + Biceps day (gym), main lift
prescription.warmup: Bar x 10, then 1 set x 5 at ~60%

steps: Eyes under the bar. Grip ~1.5x shoulder width, bar in the heel of the palm, wrist stacked.
Pinch shoulder blades down and back, small arch, upper back and glutes on the bench.
Feet flat, slightly behind knees, screwed outward.
Set safeties just below chest height. Unrack with straight arms, bar over your shoulders.
cues: Bend the bar into a U.
Push yourself away from the bar into the bench.
Drive the floor away and press the bar back toward the rack.

biomechanics.forceVector: Bar path is a slight J: down to the sternum, then up and back over the shoulders.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Elbows ~45-60° from the torso at the bottom; forearms vertical when viewed from the side.
biomechanics.momentArm: Tucking the elbows shortens the shoulder moment arm and keeps the bar over the elbow, so less shear on the shoulder and more force into the bar.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Floor → legs → glutes → braced trunk → scapulae → humerus → bar.
biomechanics.grf: Leg drive is horizontal force that drives your upper back into the bench; it raises force output without the hips leaving the bench.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Just off the chest to mid-range (the 'sticking point' a few cm up).

neural.intent: Control down, then try to accelerate the bar the entire way up.
neural.rfd: Moving heavy loads with max intent teaches you to recruit high-threshold motor units fast.

powerPair.rest: 5-7 min after the top set, then go

cards.mobility: Full touch-and-press range loads the pec and anterior shoulder at length — builds shoulder extension and thoracic extension under control.
cards.footBase: Tripod foot on the floor, then screw the feet outward without moving them. Glutes fire, your knees stop collapsing in, and the leg drive actually reaches the bar instead of leaking through soft, flat arches.
cards.sequencing: Leg drive starts before the bar leaves the chest: feet → glutes → trunk → bar.

looks.effect: Full chest, front delt and triceps thickness — the general 'built' look.
looks.lengthened: Touch the chest every rep with no bounce; don't cut range to lift more.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Max horizontal push strength: line play, stiff-arms, pushing off an opponent in the clinch, framing.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Raises your force ceiling. Pair with plyo push-ups or the strength won't show up in punches.

intensityTechnique.technique: None on heavy sets; optional 1 back-off set of 8-10 at -20%, last rep at 1 RIR

tips.tip: Stop sets at ~20% rep-speed loss instead of grinding — the slow grinding reps hurt power more than they help strength.
Rest 3 min between heavy sets; shorter rest cuts load and strength gains.
Never bench to failure without safeties or a spotter; otherwise leave 1 RIR.
Don't ice/cold-water after this session — post-lifting cold water blunted long-term muscle and strength gains.

cards.teachMe: The bench is a full-body lift disguised as an upper-body lift. Your nervous system scales output to how stable the base feels — loose feet and shoulder blades make your brain hold back. Physics: pressing force has to travel through a stiff chain from floor to bar. Any loose link absorbs force instead of passing it on.

swaps.home: Dumbbell floor press with a 1-s pause on the floor, 12-20 reps with your light DBs.
swaps.bodyweight: Weighted-backpack push-up or deficit push-up, 6-15 reps.

cards.name: Deficit Push-Up
equipment: 2 dumbbells or books/chairs for the deficit
cards.doThisNotThat: Put your hands on dumbbells or books so your chest sinks below your hands — a normal push-up stops before the pecs get the deep stretch.
cards.priorityNote: Home staple: hits looks (chest) and athleticism (serratus, trunk stiffness) with zero equipment.

prescription.reps: 8-20 (to 1-2 RIR); add a backpack load when you pass 20
prescription.load: Bodyweight; 1-2 RIR, last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s down, 1 s pause at the bottom, push explosively
prescription.slot: Chest + Biceps day (home main press) or finisher at the gym

steps: Hands on two dumbbells (neutral grip) or book stacks 8-15 cm high, slightly wider than shoulders.
Body in a straight line: squeeze glutes, ribs down, chin tucked.
Elbows ~45° from the torso, not flared.
Lower until your chest is level with or below your hands.
cues: Push the floor away from you.
Spread the floor apart with your hands.
Keep your body a rigid plank from head to heels.

biomechanics.forceVector: You push the floor; reaction force goes up through your hands. ~65-70% of bodyweight is on your hands in a standard push-up.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Elbows ~45° from torso; body straight; shoulders over or just behind the hands at the bottom.
biomechanics.momentArm: Deeper range = bigger shoulder horizontal-abduction angle = more pec stretch under load.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Hands → serratus/scapula → trunk (anti-extension) → glutes → feet. The trunk has to be a stiff beam.
biomechanics.grf: Push the floor down and slightly back; the reaction force drives you up and forward.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The bottom 5 cm below hand level.

neural.intent: Slow down, explode up — push hard enough that you almost leave the handles.
neural.rfd: Explosive intent recruits fast-twitch fibers and trains you to apply force fast.

powerPair.rest: Directly after each set, 15-20 s

cards.elastic: Working sets: pause at the bottom to kill the bounce. Power pairing: quick drop and rebound uses the stretch-shortening cycle.
cards.mobility: The deficit loads the pecs and front shoulders at long lengths — direct ROM work for your tight chest and shoulders.
cards.sequencing: Push with the whole body — glutes and trunk locked so your hips rise at the same speed as your shoulders.

looks.effect: Builds chest, front delts and triceps while the full plank keeps the core tight.
looks.lengthened: Spend 1 s at the deepest point; on the last set, 5 partials in the bottom half.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Closed-chain push with trunk stiffness: getting up off the mat, posting, sprawl recovery, contact in football.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Serratus anterior protracts the shoulder blade — the last few cm of a straight punch. Finish each rep by pushing the floor an extra centimeter away.

intensityTechnique.technique: Mechanical drop set: deficit to failure → regular push-up → knee push-up

tips.tip: Finish every rep with an extra push at the top (protraction) — that's serratus work, and serratus sets the shoulder blade for straight punches.
Near-failure bodyweight sets grow muscle similarly to heavier lifting when effort is high.
A backpack with books is a real loading tool — add weight when you pass 20 reps.
Neutral-grip handles (dumbbells) reduce wrist extension stress, letting you train deeper without wrist pain.

cards.teachMe: Your body can only push with what your trunk can transfer — a sagging hip is a broken link, and force leaks out of it. That's the same chain as a punch: ground to fist through a stiff body. The deficit adds range, which loads the pec where it's stretched, and that's a strong growth signal.

swaps.home: Backpack-loaded deficit push-up on dumbbells.
swaps.bodyweight: Deficit push-up between two chairs; regress to incline push-up if needed.

cards.name: Plyometric Push-Up
cards.doThisNotThat: Stop each set the moment you don't leave the floor — sloppy, slow plyo reps train slowness.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism first: this is the upper-body power transfer for punching.

prescription.load: Bodyweight; every rep max height; end the set when height drops
prescription.rest: 60-90 s (full recovery, this is about speed)
prescription.tempo: Quick dip, explode
prescription.slot: Power pairing after the main press, or start of Chest day

steps: Push-up position, hands slightly wider than shoulders.
Brace glutes and trunk — rigid plank.
Drop a few cm fast and push hard enough to leave the floor.
Land softly with bent elbows and go straight into the next rep.
cues: Punch the floor away.
Get as high off the floor as possible.
Land quiet.

biomechanics.forceVector: Vertical push; to leave the floor, force must exceed body-weight share on the hands.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Elbows ~45° from torso; shallow dip (~1/3 depth) for faster ground contact.
biomechanics.momentArm: Shorter dip = shorter shoulder moment arm = faster turnaround.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Floor → hands → shoulders → trunk → glutes. Sagging hips absorb force.
biomechanics.grf: Bigger, faster push = bigger reaction force = more airtime.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The transition from lowering to pushing (the amortization phase).

neural.intent: Maximal speed on every rep.
neural.rfd: Pure RFD work: how fast you hit peak force, the same quality as punch snap.

powerPair.exercise: This IS the power pairing (pair after incline/bench press)
powerPair.rest: Do it ~4-6 min after the heavy set

cards.elastic: Fast drop → fast push = stretch-shortening cycle; the pec and anterior shoulder tendons store and return energy. Short ground contact is the goal.
cards.mobility: Minor — ROM here is shallow on purpose. Your mobility work comes from the deep presses.
cards.sequencing: Rigid trunk, glutes squeezed, so the push travels into the floor and back up as one piece.

looks.effect: Small direct effect; trains fast-twitch fibers, which have the most growth potential.
looks.lengthened: Not applicable — power drill.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Upper-body rate of force development: punches, stiff-arms, chest passes.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Punch snap is RFD, not max strength. This is the drill that turns bench strength into punching power.

intensityTechnique.technique: None — quality only

tips.tip: End the set when you slow down — velocity-loss caps protect power adaptations.
Pair with a heavy press: power expression usually peaks several minutes after the heavy set, not seconds after.
External focus ("push the floor away") beats internal ("use your chest") for speed.
Skip the clap until you reliably land softly — wrists and face take the hit from bad landings.

cards.teachMe: Strength is how much force you can make; power is how fast. Your nervous system learns speed only when you practice speed — every slow rep teaches it to be slow. Short, explosive sets teach the brain to recruit fast fibers all at once.

swaps.home: Same — bodyweight only.
swaps.bodyweight: Incline plyo push-up on a couch arm if you can't leave the floor yet.

cards.name: Cable / Dumbbell Fly
cards.doThisNotThat: Use cables (or low-incline DBs) and stretch deep with a soft elbow — don't do heavy DB flys where the top is dead tension and you can't control the stretch.
cards.priorityNote: Looks priority — chest growth at long lengths. Kept low volume so it doesn't steal from power work.

prescription.load: Last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lower into the stretch, 1 s pause, squeeze up
prescription.slot: Chest + Biceps day, accessory after presses

steps: Cables at shoulder height (or slightly above), one step forward, split stance.
Slight elbow bend locked (~15-20°).
Open arms until you feel a strong chest stretch with hands slightly behind the torso line.
Bring hands together in front of the lower chest.
cues: Hug a big tree.
Lead with your elbows, not the handles.
Drive your back foot into the floor.

biomechanics.forceVector: Cables pull back and out, so tension stays on through the whole arc; dumbbells pull straight down, so tension disappears at the top.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Elbow fixed ~15-20°; shoulder horizontal abduction to just past the torso line.
biomechanics.momentArm: Long arm = long moment arm on the shoulder, so light weights feel heavy. Max moment arm with DBs is at the bottom.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Split stance → braced trunk → scapulae pinned → humerus.
biomechanics.grf: Back foot pushes into the floor; that stabilizes the trunk against the cable pull.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: The stretched (wide) position.

neural.intent: Controlled stretch, then drive the hands together hard.
neural.rfd: Low priority here — it's a growth exercise.

cards.mobility: Direct loaded stretch for tight pecs/anterior shoulder — improves your shoulder opening (horizontal abduction), useful for your all-over stiffness.
cards.footBase: Split stance with the front foot in a tripod and both feet screwed into the floor; your arches stay up and the trunk doesn't rotate with the cable.

looks.effect: Inner and mid chest fullness.
looks.lengthened: The deep stretch is the money position: last set, 5-8 partials in the stretched half.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Horizontal adduction strength: bear-hugs, body locks, pulling an opponent in.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Body lock and clinch squeeze use this pattern; the punching chain needs the pressing work instead.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials
intensityTechnique.when: Last set, after failure on full reps

tips.tip: Lengthened partials are at least as good as full reps for growth; add them after full-ROM failure for extra stimulus.
Cables keep tension on at the top — DB flys lose tension when the arms are vertical.
Low-incline DB flys (15-30°) put more tension on the upper chest.

cards.teachMe: A long lever arm makes light weights heavy, so flys need to be light and controlled. The stretched position is where the pec is under the most tension at long length, and that's a big growth signal. Don't chase heavy weight here — chase stretch and control.

swaps.home: Floor DB fly (elbows touch the floor = safe stretch limit) with light DBs, 12-20 reps.
swaps.bodyweight: Towel or sliding push-up fly on a smooth floor, partial range.

cards.name: Incline Dumbbell Curl
cards.doThisNotThat: Curl lying back on a 45-60° incline with the arms hanging BEHIND the torso and the elbow pinned in space. Most people stand, swing, and let the elbow drift forward, which shortens the long head before the rep even starts.
cards.priorityNote: Looks wins here (arm size); athleticism comes from the press/pull and power work, so this stays a 2-3 set accessory, never a priority lift.

prescription.reps: 8-12 (double progression: hit 12 on all sets → +5 lb or slower lowering)
prescription.load: 1-2 RIR on sets 1-2, failure on the last set. Light home DBs are enough: the stretched start makes 10-20 lb hard.
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lower, 1 s dead-stop at full stretch, max-intent curl up (no swing)
prescription.slot: Chest + Biceps day, accessory after presses and power work

steps: Bench at 45-60° (lower = more stretch; start at 60° if your shoulders are stiff).
Upper back and head on the pad, feet flat in a tripod, ribs down.
Arms hang straight down, slightly behind the torso line, palms forward.
Curl by moving only the forearm; the elbow stays at the same spot in space for the whole rep.
Lower to a fully straight elbow with the shoulder still back; pause 1 s, then curl.
cues: Point your elbows at the floor the whole rep.
Bring the pinky edge of the bell up toward the ceiling at the top.
Let the bells hang to the floor at the bottom until the arm is dead straight.

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls the DB straight down; the biceps flexes the elbow against it. Because the torso is reclined, the start of the rep is easy-ish and the loaded range shifts toward mid-range and the top.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder extended ~20-30° behind the torso; elbow from 0° (straight) to ~130°. The long head crosses the shoulder, so shoulder extension + straight elbow = its longest length.
biomechanics.momentArm: Torque = DB weight × horizontal distance from elbow to hand. Peak when the forearm is horizontal; near zero at the very bottom and top. Elbow drifting forward shortens the moment arm and steals tension.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Pad pins the scapula → humerus fixed → only the elbow moves. Zero leg drive or torso swing is possible, which is the point: pure elbow-flexor demand.
biomechanics.grf: Minimal. Feet in a tripod just stop you sliding; the bench is the base.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Forearm horizontal (max moment arm), with the long head still fairly long. The bottom is the stretch, not the hardest point.

neural.intent: Control the lowering, then curl up as fast as the load allows. Intent to accelerate recruits high-threshold motor units even when the bar moves slowly.
neural.rfd: Low priority. This is a looks lift; the power work for the day is the plyo push-up or med-ball throw.
