cards.mobility: Loaded shoulder extension with a straight elbow stretches the front of the shoulder and the long head. This is the stiff range that pulls your shoulders forward. Full-ROM loading builds range about as well as stretching (Afonso 2021), so every rep is mobility work.
cards.footBase: Seated, but feet still matter: tripod feet flat and light Screw pressure into the floor. That pins the pelvis so the lower back doesn't arch and the shoulders stay on the pad.

looks.effect: Biceps peak and fullness from the front; arms look bigger in a T-shirt when the long head (outer biceps) fills out.
looks.lengthened: Bottom position: shoulder behind the body + elbow fully straight = long head at its longest. Last set: after failure, 5-6 partials in the bottom third only.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Elbow flexors decelerate the arm after throws, serves and swings (eccentric braking), and they power pulling and gripping. A stronger long head also helps the front of the shoulder resist the stretch it takes at full layback.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Collar ties, underhooks pulling in, and finishing a rear-naked choke all need elbow flexion under load. It does NOT add punch power. Punches are elbow extension driven by the hips, so this stays an accessory.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials after failure (5-6 bottom-third reps)

tips.tip: Shoulder extension pre-stretches the long head because it crosses the shoulder. Training at long muscle lengths grew muscle as much as or more than short-range training in several trials; recent work points to parity with full ROM, so take the stretch as a free bonus.
Stop the rep when the elbow starts moving forward. That movement is the front delt taking over and shortening the long head, so the "extra" rep doesn't count.

Rotate the pinky up at the top. The biceps is a forearm supinator as well as an elbow flexor, so full supination gives full contraction. A neutral grip shifts the load to the brachialis (hammer curl).
Failure on the last set only. Being 1-3 reps from failure grows muscle about as well (Refalo 2023), and grinding every set wrecks the next day's pulling.
0.5-8 s reps grow similarly (Schoenfeld 2015). The 1-s pause at the bottom is there to kill bounce from the stretch, not to make the rep slower for its own sake.

cards.teachMe: The long head of the biceps starts above the shoulder joint, so when your arm sits behind your body the muscle is already stretched before the elbow bends. That is a position the nervous system rarely gets loaded in, so the brain treats it as unsafe and tenses up. Slow, controlled reps there teach it the range is safe, and it gives back some of the shoulder range your posture took. The physics: torque is weight × horizontal distance, so the elbow must stay still. Let it drift forward and you shorten the lever, cut the tension, and turn the lift into a front-delt raise.

swaps.home: Floor or couch-edge incline curl: lie back on the couch arm or a pile of cushions at ~45° with arms hanging behind the torso. Same light DBs, 3-s lowering + pause; if you get 15+ easy reps, add bottom-third partials.
swaps.bodyweight: Towel door-handle curl: towel around a sturdy door handle (door closed, you on the hinge side), lean back with straight arms behind the line of the body, curl yourself up. Walk your feet forward to make it harder.

cards.name: Hammer Curl
cards.doThisNotThat: Keep a dead-neutral wrist (thumb up, knuckles in line with the forearm) and the elbow pinned at your side. Most people curl with a bent wrist and swing the elbow forward, which turns it into a sloppy front-raise.
cards.priorityNote: Looks first (forearm thickness and arm width from the front), then grip and clinch strength. Accessory volume only; it never replaces power or main-lift work.

prescription.reps: 8-15 (double progression: 15 on all sets → +5 lb, or 3-s lowering if DBs are maxed)
prescription.load: 1-2 RIR, last set to failure. Usually 5-10 lb heavier than your supinated curl.
prescription.rest: 90 s (superset with incline curl: 60 s between the two, 90 s after the pair)
prescription.tempo: 2 s lower, no pause, max-intent up; no swing
prescription.slot: Chest + Biceps day, last accessory (or the Back + Triceps day for grip)

steps: Stand with tripod feet hip-width, light Screw into the floor, knees soft, ribs stacked over the pelvis.
DBs at your sides, palms facing the thighs (thumbs forward). Squeeze the handle hard.
Curl until the top end of the DB reaches shoulder height while the elbow stays beside the ribs.
Lower to a fully straight elbow without letting the wrist bend or the shoulders roll forward.
cues: Lead with the thumb end of the dumbbell toward the ceiling.
Elbows stay glued to your sides like they're pinned to your ribs.
Crush the handle like you're wringing water out of it.

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls straight down; the elbow flexes against it. The neutral forearm puts the brachioradialis at its best leverage, and the brachialis (pure elbow flexor, attaches to the ulna) works hard regardless of grip.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Elbow 0° → ~130°, forearm neutral (mid-pronation), wrist neutral, shoulder at ~0° (beside the torso).
biomechanics.momentArm: Torque = DB weight × horizontal distance from elbow to hand; peak at a horizontal forearm. Elbow drifting forward or a bent wrist shortens the lever and leaks force, so the same DB gives less stimulus.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet in a tripod → glutes and brace lock the pelvis → shoulder packed → the elbow is the only joint moving. Any hip swing means force from the legs is doing the curl.
biomechanics.grf: Standing: push the floor evenly through big toe, pinky toe and heel. If the arch collapses, the knees cave and the torso sways, which turns into a cheat swing.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Forearm horizontal (90° elbow).

neural.intent: Max-intent up, controlled down. A hard grip squeeze recruits more motor units in the forearm and elbow flexors (irradiation), so the curl and the grip train together.
neural.rfd: Low priority. Grip RFD matters for grabbing a wrist or collar fast, but it comes from fight drills; this lift builds the base strength.

cards.mobility: Full elbow extension at the bottom under load keeps the elbow from losing its last few degrees (common in lifters who only half-rep). Standing tall with ribs down trains posture under load.
cards.footBase: Tripod foot + the Screw: rotate the planted feet outward without moving them. The arch appears, glutes switch on, and the pelvis locks, so the swing disappears and the arms get the work.

looks.effect: Thicker forearms and brachialis. The brachialis sits under the biceps and pushes it up, so the arm looks wider from the front and side. Forearms are on show in every T-shirt.
looks.lengthened: Fully straight elbow at the bottom, shoulders back (not rolled forward). Last set: 5-6 bottom-half partials, or finish with a 20-30 s dead-hang-style DB hold at your side for grip.

sportTransfer.mechanism: The neutral-grip elbow flexion is the same line as holding a bat, racket or paddle and pulling an opponent. Grip and brachioradialis strength steady the wrist at contact, so fewer mishits come from the racket twisting in your hand.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Clinch, collar ties, two-on-one, and gripping a wrist all use thumb-up elbow flexion plus a crushing grip. Thicker forearms and stronger grip control mean you hold positions longer before forearm pump. It does not add punch power.

intensityTechnique.technique: Mechanical drop set: hammer curl to failure → immediately cross-body hammer curls → bottom-half partials

tips.tip: The brachialis is a pure elbow flexor. It works in every grip, so hammer curls hit it with whatever load you can handle, and a bigger brachialis makes the arm look wider.
Cross-body variation (DB toward the opposite pec) keeps tension on the brachialis and lets you go slightly heavier without swinging. Alternate it week to week with standard hammers.
A hard grip squeeze makes the whole arm work harder (irradiation), so grip is trained for free. No extra wrist-roller work needed for a fighter at your level.
Last set to failure only; 1-3 RIR on the others grows the same (Refalo 2023) and saves forearm recovery for fight drills and pulling.
Rest 90 s even on arms. Longer rest let trained lifters do more work and showed more growth (Schoenfeld 2016); supersetting biceps work doesn't change that for this lift.

cards.teachMe: The forearm has two bones, and the grip decides which elbow flexor is in the best position: palms up favors the biceps, thumbs up gives the brachioradialis its best leverage, and the brachialis works in every grip. That is why the hammer curl builds forearm and arm thickness the regular curl misses. A crushing grip spreads the nervous system's drive into the nearby muscles (irradiation), so the whole chain from hand to shoulder fires as one unit. That is the same unit you use to hold a collar tie or a racket at contact.

swaps.home: Same lift with light home DBs. When 15 reps gets easy, use a 3-s lowering, add the cross-body version, or do a mechanical drop set (standard → cross-body → partials).
swaps.bodyweight: Towel hammer curl: loop a towel around a door handle, hold both ends with thumbs up, lean back and curl yourself in. Or towel isometric holds: hold the bottom of the towel with a foot and pull up against it at 90° for 3 x 20 s.

cards.name: Pull-Up
cards.doThisNotThat: Start every rep from a true dead hang and pull the shoulder blades down BEFORE the elbows bend — half-reps from bent arms skip the stretch and turn it into a biceps exercise.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism + looks tie: relative strength (your bodyweight) and lat width both win, so this leads Back day when a bar is available.

prescription.reps: 4-8; at 3 x 8 add 2.5-5 lb in a backpack
prescription.load: Bodyweight to weighted; 1-2 RIR, end the set when the chin stops clearing at full speed
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lower to a full dead hang, 1 s hang, explode up
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day, first main lift after CNS prime
prescription.warmup: 1 set x 3-5 jumping negatives or chin-ups at an easy RIR 4

steps: Grip just outside shoulder width, palms forward (palms toward you = chin-up, more biceps, also fine).
Dead hang, then pull the shoulder blades down ~3-5 cm without bending the arms — a 'scap pull'.
Ribs down, glutes tight, legs straight and slightly in front — a hollow body, no swinging.
Pull until the chin clears the bar; lower all the way to a straight-arm hang.
cues: Drive your elbows down into your back pockets.
Pull the bar down to your collarbone.
Try to bend the bar into a U.

biomechanics.forceVector: Pure vertical: you lift 100% of bodyweight (~125-135 lb) straight up against gravity. Every lb of fat or loose swing is extra load.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder travels from ~170-180° flexion (overhead) to ~0-20°; elbows from straight to ~120° flexion. Torso tilts back only ~10-20° at the top.
biomechanics.momentArm: The lats have their worst leverage at the dead hang (arm overhead) and best as the elbow passes the ribs — which is why the bottom feels hardest and why people cheat it.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Hands → forearms → elbow flexors → lats/teres → scapulae (depress + retract) → hollow trunk → legs. A kip or arched back breaks the chain at the trunk.
biomechanics.grf: No ground: the bar is your 'floor'. Squeezing the bar hard (irradiation) stiffens the whole arm so force from the lats isn't lost at the hand.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: First third off the dead hang, where the lats are longest and leverage is worst.

neural.intent: Controlled 2-3 s lowering, then try to fly over the bar — accelerate the whole way up.
neural.rfd: Max-intent pulling recruits high-threshold motor units in the lats; speed of the pull is the athletic quality you keep.

powerPair.exercise: Bodyweight sprawl-to-jump (or med-ball overhead slam at the gym)
powerPair.rest: Start ~4-6 min after your top set; 60-90 s between power sets

cards.mobility: The 1 s dead hang is a loaded overhead stretch for lats, pecs and the thoracic spine — exactly where your 'stiff everywhere' shows up overhead. Loaded full-ROM work builds ROM about as well as static stretching (Afonso 2021).
cards.sequencing: Scap first, elbows second: shoulder blades depress, THEN the arms pull. Same proximal-to-distal order as every throw and punch — big muscles near the trunk start, the arm finishes.

looks.effect: Lat width is the V in V-taper; the pull-up also thickens the lower traps and arms.
looks.lengthened: Hang 1 s at the bottom with arms fully straight and shoulders elevated; on the last set add 3-5 bottom-half partials (dead hang to forehead height) after failure.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Vertical pulling strength and bodyweight control: pulling yourself to an opponent, climbing to the back in BJJ, the lat-driven downswing of a volleyball spike and baseball throw deceleration.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Lats pull the elbow back to your side — the punch retraction that resets your guard. Strong lats also mean you can drag an opponent's head down in the clinch.

intensityTechnique.technique: Negatives: after the last full rep, jump to the top and lower over 3-5 s, 2-3 times

tips.tip: Can't do 4 strict reps yet? Jumping negatives (3-5 s lower) build the strength fastest; skip band assistance — you don't own bands anyway.
Rest the full 2.5-3 min; your second and third set will have ~1-3 more reps than with 1-min rest.
Stop when the chin stops clearing at full speed — grinding to 40% velocity loss gave smaller jump gains than stopping at 20% in squats; same logic for pulling power.
Thinking 'elbows to pockets' (external) beats 'squeeze your lats' (internal) for performance.
Light bodyweight is an advantage here — at ~130 lb, relative strength builds fast; aim for 10 strict reps, then load it.

cards.teachMe: Your brain decides how hard you're allowed to pull based on how safe the joint feels. Starting from a dead hang with the shoulder blades set tells it the shoulder is locked in, so it releases more of the lat. Physics: at the bottom the lat's line of pull is nearly parallel to the arm, so it has terrible leverage — that's why the first few cm are hardest and why owning them builds the most strength.

swaps.home: No bar at home: one-arm DB row with a 3 s lower + 1 s stretch, 10-15 reps per side, plus doorway or table rows.
swaps.bodyweight: Table inverted row: lie under a sturdy table, grip the edge, body straight, pull your chest to the table; elevate feet on a chair to make it harder.

studies: Afonso 2021 (strength training vs stretching for ROM)

cards.name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row
cards.doThisNotThat: Pull the dumbbell in an arc toward your hip, not straight up to your armpit — the hip path trains the lats; the armpit path turns it into a shrug.
cards.priorityNote: Athleticism + looks: the anti-rotation demand is fight-relevant and it's your best home back builder.

prescription.reps: 6-12 per side (light home DBs: 12-20 with the 3 s lower)
prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; stop when your torso starts twisting to finish the rep
prescription.rest: 2 min per side cycle (work side A, rest ~60 s, side B, rest ~60 s)
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s lower, 1 s full stretch at the bottom, explode up
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day: main lift at home, second pull at the gym

steps: Same-side hand and knee on a bench (home: one hand on the couch arm, staggered stance, front knee bent).
Spine flat, hips and shoulders square to the floor.
Let the DB hang straight down so the shoulder blade slides forward — full stretch.
Pull the elbow back toward the hip, close to the ribs.
cues: Drive your elbow back toward your back pocket.
Push the bench away with your support hand.
Keep your belt buckle pointing at the floor.

biomechanics.forceVector: Gravity pulls the DB straight down; you pull back and up along an arc toward the hip, which matches the lat fibers' line of pull (shoulder extension).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Torso ~parallel to the floor (0-15°); elbow ~20-30° from the torso; the humerus moves from ~90° flexion to just past the torso line.
biomechanics.momentArm: With the torso flat, gravity acts perpendicular to the upper arm through mid-range, so the lats get max torque around shoulder extension; the free side creates a rotational torque your trunk has to resist.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Support hand + feet → anti-rotation trunk (obliques) → scapula (retract/depress) → humerus → elbow → DB.
biomechanics.grf: Support hand pushes into the bench and feet drive the floor — that ground force is what keeps the trunk from rotating toward the DB.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Top contraction, elbow just past the torso, where the moment arm is longest and the rhomboids/lats are shortest.

neural.intent: Controlled lower into a stretch, then rip the elbow back as fast as possible.
neural.rfd: Explosive single-arm pulls train fast rear-chain recruitment on one side while the trunk stays still — the punch-retraction pattern.

powerPair.exercise: Rotational DB high-pull or shadowbox 3 x 5 max-speed rear-hand retractions
powerPair.rest: Done ~4-6 min after the top set

cards.mobility: The 1 s bottom stretch pulls the shoulder blade around the rib cage and lengthens the lat — direct work against your stiff shoulders and upper back.
cards.footBase: Staggered home version: front foot in a tripod (big-toe ball, pinky-toe ball, heel), both feet screwed outward so the arch stays up and the hips stay square.
cards.sequencing: Shoulder blade starts, elbow finishes — trunk stays still. That still trunk is the base every punch and pull needs.

looks.effect: Lat thickness and width + mid-back density — the back looks 3D from the side and wide from behind.
looks.lengthened: Let the shoulder blade fully protract at the bottom (DB hangs a few cm lower than you'd think); last set, 4-6 bottom-half partials after failure.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Single-arm pulling with anti-rotation: retracting a punch, the backswing of a racket or paddle, pulling an opponent one-handed while staying square.
sportTransfer.combatNote: A fast-retracting punch closes the gap in your guard. Lats + rear delts pull it back; train them as hard as the push.

intensityTechnique.technique: Lengthened partials (bottom half) after failure on full reps

tips.tip: Pull toward the hip, not the chest — moving the path down shifts the work to the lat.
Light home DBs: slow the lower to 3 s and add a 1 s top squeeze — rep durations of 0.5-8 s grow muscle similarly, so slow tempo is a valid way to make light weights work.
Near-failure (1-3 RIR) is about as good as failure for growth — save failure for the last set.
If your torso twists to finish a rep, the set is over — that's your anti-rotation core failing, not your lats.

cards.teachMe: One arm at a time puts the weight off-center, so gravity tries to twist you. Your obliques have to resist that twist — that's the same anti-rotation stiffness that lets force travel from your hips to your fist instead of leaking out. Pulling toward the hip lines the arm up with the lat's fibers, so the force goes into the muscle you're trying to grow.

swaps.home: Same exercise with home DBs braced on a couch; add the 3 s lower and top pause.
swaps.bodyweight: Table inverted row (feet elevated to progress) or single-arm towel row on a door.

cards.name: Lat Pulldown
cards.doThisNotThat: Let the weight pull your arms fully overhead (shoulders shrug up) at the top every rep and lean back only ~10-15° — don't swing back to 45° and stop the bar halfway up.
cards.priorityNote: Looks leads (lat width) — use it when pull-ups can't be loaded or for extra back volume.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR on sets 1-2, last set to failure
prescription.tempo: 2-3 s up into a full stretch, 1 s at the top, pull fast
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day (gym), after the main pull or row

steps: Thigh pad snug so your knees can't lift.
Grip ~1.2-1.5x shoulder width, overhand (or neutral handle).
Torso back ~10-15°, chest up, ribs down.
Pull the bar to the top of your chest; let it go all the way back up.
cues: Pull your elbows down into your back pockets.
Bring the bar to your collarbone.
Let the bar stretch you tall at the top.

biomechanics.forceVector: The cable pulls up and slightly forward; you pull down and back, mostly shoulder adduction/extension.
biomechanics.jointAngles: Shoulder from ~170° flexion to ~20°; elbow from straight to ~100-120° flexion; torso lean 10-15°.
biomechanics.momentArm: The cable keeps tension near-constant, but the lats' leverage is worst overhead — so the top stretch is where light weight feels heavy.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet → thigh pad → braced trunk → scapulae (depress) → lats → elbows → hands.
biomechanics.grf: Feet flat and pushing into the floor pin the thighs under the pad — a stable base means the pull goes into the bar, not your hips lifting.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Bottom contraction (bar at the chest) for strength; top stretch for control.

neural.intent: Controlled up, then pull the bar down as fast as you can.
neural.rfd: Moderate; it's an accessory, so intent matters more than speed tracking.

cards.mobility: The full overhead stretch lengthens the lats, which are one of the main things that block your overhead reach (a big contributor to the stiff feeling in your shoulders).
cards.footBase: Feet flat in a tripod and screwed outward — the push into the floor locks the thighs under the pad and stops your arches from collapsing.
cards.sequencing: Shoulder blades drop first, then the elbows pull. Proximal before distal, every rep.

looks.effect: Lat width = the V in the V-taper.
looks.lengthened: Hold 1 s with arms fully straight and shoulders up at the top; last set, 5-8 top-half partials after failure.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Vertical pulling strength with a stable trunk: dragging an opponent's head down, the downstroke of a spike, the lat contribution to throwing.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Lats pull the elbow to the ribs — the same motion that keeps your elbows tight to block body shots and drags a collar tie down.

intensityTechnique.technique: Drop set (~30% off) then top-half lengthened partials

tips.tip: Pause at the top stretch — training at long muscle lengths tends to grow as well as or better than short ranges.
Thumbless grip (thumb on the same side as the fingers) often reduces forearm fatigue so the lats fail first.
Cue 'elbows to pockets', not 'squeeze the lats' — external focus improves performance.
Rest 2 min; shorter rest reduces reps on later sets.

cards.teachMe: Your lats run from your upper arm all the way down to your pelvis. When your arm goes fully overhead they're stretched along their whole length, which is a strong growth signal and teaches the nervous system the overhead range is safe. The more range it trusts, the less it grips — that's how strength work loosens you up.

swaps.home: One-arm DB row (3 s lower) + floor DB pullover, 12-20 reps.
swaps.bodyweight: Table inverted row, feet elevated.

cards.name: Barbell Row
cards.doThisNotThat: Hold the hinge at ~30-45° and pull to the belly button — don't stand taller every rep until it turns into a shrug.
cards.priorityNote: Functional strength + posture; athleticism through the isometric hip hinge.

prescription.load: 1-2 RIR; set ends when the torso angle changes
prescription.tempo: 2 s lower, pull explosively
prescription.slot: Back + Triceps day (gym), main lift

steps: Feet hip-width, overhand grip just outside the shins.
Hinge to a 30-45° torso angle, knees soft (~20°).
Brace: big breath into the belly, ribs down, spine neutral.
Bar hangs under the shoulders; pull it to the lower ribs/belly button.
cues: Drive your elbows to the ceiling behind you.
Pull the bar into your belly button.
Root your feet into the floor.

biomechanics.forceVector: You pull vertically while the hinge is held; gravity also tries to round your spine forward (flexion moment).
biomechanics.jointAngles: Torso 30-45° above the floor; knees ~20°; elbows ~45° from the torso.
biomechanics.momentArm: The bar's distance in front of the hips is a long moment arm, so the spinal erectors and hamstrings work isometrically every rep.
biomechanics.kineticChain: Feet → hamstrings/glutes (isometric) → braced spine → scapulae → elbows → bar.
biomechanics.grf: Feet push the floor to hold the hinge; that's what stops your hips from popping up.
biomechanics.hardestPoint: Top contraction, bar at the belly.

neural.intent: Rip the bar up fast; control it down.
neural.rfd: Training the pull from a held hinge builds posterior-chain stiffness and fast upper-back recruitment.

powerPair.rest: ~4-6 min after the top set

cards.mobility: The held hinge loads the hamstrings at length — builds hip-hinge range, a key fix for your all-over stiffness.
cards.footBase: Tripod foot and screw outward — essential to hold the hinge without your flat arches collapsing and knees drifting in.
cards.sequencing: Hinge set first; then the shoulder blades retract, then the elbows pull.

looks.effect: Back thickness and posture — shoulders sit back, chest looks bigger.
looks.lengthened: Let the shoulder blades protract at the bottom of each rep.

sportTransfer.mechanism: Pulling from a hinged, athletic position — the same posture as a wrestling stance, a lineman's hand fight, or a front headlock.
sportTransfer.combatNote: Hinged pulling strength for front headlocks and snapping an opponent's head down.

intensityTechnique.technique: None on heavy sets; optional back-off set of 10-12 at -20%

tips.tip: The set is over when your torso angle changes — that's the hinge failing, not the back.
Rest 2.5-3 min on heavy rows; short rest cuts load.
Stop around 20% velocity loss for better power transfer.
Bracing with a big belly breath creates intra-abdominal pressure that stiffens the spine — hold it through the pull.

cards.teachMe: The barbell row teaches your back to pull while your hips and spine hold an athletic hinge — the position you're in for almost every sport. Physics: the bar out in front creates a long lever on your lower back, so your brain has to learn to hold the trunk stiff while the arms move. That stiff-trunk, moving-limbs pattern is the core of every athletic movement.

swaps.home: One-arm DB row or two-DB chest-supported row on an incline.
swaps.bodyweight: Table inverted row.

morning5.name: Morning 5
rules: Barefoot, every morning, right after waking. Half-hearted counts.
No pain, no forcing end range: move to a comfortable stretch, breathe, come back.
If you only have 2 minutes: do steps 1, 3 and 6.

steps.dose: 5 × 5 s per foot, seated or standing
steps.why: Pull the ball of the foot toward the heel without curling the toes, lifting the arch. Directly trains the small arch muscles that flat feet underuse. Meta-analysis shows a real but small effect on navicular drop.

steps.dose: 10 reps: big toe up / others down, then switch
steps.why: Restores independent toe control, which the tripod foot needs to grip the ground.

steps.drill: The Screw hold in ready position
steps.why: Rotate both feet outward into the floor without moving them: the arch rises, glutes fire, knees line up. Installs the flat-foot correction you'll use in every standing lift and sport.

steps.dose: 10 per side, slow
steps.why: Ankle dorsiflexion is usually limited with flat feet and causes knees to cave. Rocking the knee over the 2nd toe toward the wall restores range under control.

steps.dose: 8 switches, hands behind you
steps.why: Rotates both hips through internal and external rotation; moving actively through the range builds ROM similarly to stretching (Afonso 2021).

steps.dose: 5 per side, breathe out as you open
steps.why: A stiff upper back forces the shoulders and arm to rotate alone, feeding arm-first sequencing. Opening the thoracic spine lets the trunk rotate as one link in the chain.

steps.dose: 5 breaths: 4 s in through nose, 6-8 s out
steps.why: Long exhales shift the nervous system out of the protective, grip-everything state, which is part of why you feel stiff everywhere.

morning5.teachMe: Your stiffness is partly protection: the brain limits range when it doesn't trust the base (collapsed arches) or senses threat. These 5 minutes give it a stable foot, a reminder that each joint can move safely, and a calm breath, so it gradually loosens the brake. Strength through full range builds mobility about as well as stretching (Afonso 2021), so your loaded lifts keep this going all day.

steps.drill: Box breathing 4-4-4-4, then wall push isometric 'release the brake'
steps.dose: 3 breath cycles, then 2 × 6 s max-intent wall push in an athletic split stance
steps.why: The slow exhale downshifts the threat state that makes you freeze then react late. The 6 s max push tells the nervous system that high force is safe, so more fast-twitch units come online for the first sprint.

steps.dose: 20 s near-far (thumb → rim), then 10 tosses of the ball toward your face that you catch at chest
steps.why: Eyes are the first link in the chain. A ball coming straight at you is the threat cue; catching 10 easy ones teaches the brain it's safe, so it stops flinching and grabbing on passes.

steps.drill: The Screw into ready position + pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw holds (feet planted, rotate outward into the floor), then 2 × 15 pogos
steps.why: Flat feet let the arch collapse, ankle roll in and knee cave. The Screw torques the arch up and fires glutes; pogos then stiffen the Achilles spring so the first step bounces instead of sinks.

steps.dose: 6 closeouts (sprint 3 steps, chop, land and freeze 1 s in ready position: knees ~25°, hips hinged ~15°), 2 × 4 slides each way
steps.why: Freezing 1 s on every landing burns a balanced stop into the motor map, so you stop reaching and lunging and your feet are under you on defense without thinking.

steps.dose: 10 one-hand shots from 3 ft, then 10 from the elbow: legs push, ball leaves at the top
steps.why: Your sequencing fires arm-first. Close shots where the legs clearly start the motion re-order the chain: ground → hips → shoulder → wrist, so the release is the last link of the whip.

steps.dose: 3 × baseline-to-half-court at 60/80/95%, then 3 two-foot rebound jumps touching as high as possible
steps.why: Ramping intensity gives a variable-intensity warm-up (airways) and recruits high-threshold motor units so the first possession isn't your slowest.

pregame.anchorCue: Between possessions: two quick bounces, land in ready.
pregame.airwayNote: Basketball is stop-start high intensity, a classic EIB trigger. The build-up sprints double as a variable-intensity warm-up, which reduced the post-exercise lung-function drop in a systematic review (Stickland 2012, grade B); protection lasts roughly 1-2 h for many people (some see up to ~2-4 h). Keep sprints short: aim for HR ~170-185 (≈85-90% of max ~200-205) for brief bursts, then walk. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static stretches (>30 s per muscle) right before playing
Heavy lifting or max-rep jumps before the game
Thinking about form during play: the patterns are installed now
pregame.teachMe: Speed on the court is mostly perception plus a stiff, well-aligned base. Your eyes set how early you can act and your feet set how fast you can push. This protocol primes both: it calms the threat response so vision opens up, then lines up the foot-knee-hip stack so ground reaction force goes straight up the chain instead of leaking through a collapsed arch.

steps.dose: 3 slow breaths (4 s in nose, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: A long exhale turns off the gripping, protective tension that makes swings stiff. The isometric primes maximal recruitment without fatigue.

steps.dose: 20 s fast eye jumps between two targets ~1 m apart, then 10 underhand tosses toward your face from a partner/wall that you track to the glove
steps.why: Hitting and fielding fail on the eyes first. Tracking an approaching ball all the way in teaches the brain the ball is safe, which kills the flinch that makes contact random.

steps.drill: The Screw in batting stance + tripod rock
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw holds in stance, 5 slow rocks onto back-leg tripod (big toe, pinky toe, heel)
steps.why: A flat back foot rolls in and dumps the load before the swing starts. Screwing the feet into the ground loads the back hip so rotation can start from the floor.

steps.dose: 8 Hip Snaps (bat across shoulders, load back hip, snap hips to face the pitcher, hands stay back), then 8 dry swings at 70%
steps.why: Your arm fires first and the body catches up late. Hip Snaps with the hands locked force the order ground → hips → trunk → arms, so the bat becomes the last, fastest link of the whip.

steps.dose: 3 dry swings each at low / middle / high contact, then 6 ground-ball shuffles to the side, stick 1 s, throw
steps.why: Swinging through three reference heights calibrates bat path, so you're not guessing. Sticking the field-and-set position teaches feet-before-arm on the throw.

steps.dose: 10 throws building 50 → 90% distance, then 2 × 20 m sprints at 80/95%
steps.why: Arm tissues and the shoulder need graded load before max throws, and short sprints wake up the fast-twitch fibers for base running.

pregame.anchorCue: Between pitches: feel both feet screw into the dirt.
avoid: Max-effort throws or swings in the first minute
Long static stretching of the shoulder or hamstrings right before
Weighted-bat donut swings as a warm-up: they temporarily distort bat-speed feel
pregame.teachMe: A swing is a ground-to-bat energy transfer. Each link (feet, hips, trunk, arms) speeds up and then brakes so the next link goes faster, like cracking a whip. If the arm leads, the big engines (legs, hips) never get to contribute and contact is random. You're installing the order now so the game doesn't need you to think.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push from a 3-point-style lean
steps.why: Down-regulates the threat state so you read plays instead of freezing. The lean isometric rehearses the exact body angle of a drive.

steps.dose: 10 tosses toward your face caught at chest, then 6 catches where you stare at a fixed point and catch a ball tossed from the side
steps.why: Catching starts with letting the ball come to you without a flinch. Peripheral catches train the wide-field vision you use for reading defenders.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 15 pogos, 2 × 10 m A-skips
steps.why: Your arch collapses under load. The Screw sets a stiff tripod and the pogos stiffen the ankle spring, so the first step drives instead of sinking.

steps.dose: 6 cuts (3 each way): 5 m jog, plant, freeze 1 s with knee over the 2nd toe, go
steps.why: Freezing the plant installs knee-over-foot alignment, which counters valgus caused by flat feet and makes cuts sharper and safer.

steps.drill: Hip-led throws (if QB/throwing) or route stems
steps.dose: 8 throws at 60% stepping toward the target with hips opening first, or 4 routes at 70%
steps.why: Hips-then-arm sequencing adds distance with less arm stress; route stems groove deceleration mechanics before game speed.

steps.dose: 3 × 20 m at 70/85/95%, walk back
steps.why: Graded speed recruits high-threshold motor units and doubles as an interval-style warm-up for your airways.

pregame.anchorCue: In your stance: tripod feet, then go.
pregame.airwayNote: Repeated sprints are a common EIB trigger. Short build-up sprints act as an interval-style warm-up, which cut the post-exercise drop in lung function in a systematic review (Stickland 2012, grade B), with protection lasting roughly 1-2 h. Brief bursts to HR ~170-185, then walk. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static stretches before
Full-contact drills as a warm-up
New tackling technique on game day
pregame.teachMe: Acceleration is a force-angle problem: you need to push the ground backward and down while leaning forward, and a collapsing foot wastes that push sideways. Priming the foot and the eyes first means the push goes straight through the chain and the read happens earlier.

steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s nose in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Lowers threat arousal so your touch is soft, and recruits more muscle for the first sprint.

steps.dose: 20 s quick head-and-eye scans left-right, 20 s near-far (ball at feet → far goal)
steps.why: Good players scan before receiving. Fast eye shifts wake up the visual system so you see pressure early instead of reacting late.

steps.drill: The Screw + single-leg tripod balance + pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 20 s per leg on tripod foot, 2 × 15 pogos
steps.why: Every pass and shot is on one leg. A stable tripod on the plant foot stops the ankle rolling in, so energy goes into the ball instead of into wobble.

steps.dose: 6 plant-and-freeze (1 s) cuts, then 20 one-touch wall passes alternating feet
steps.why: Freezing on the plant installs a balanced base; one-touch passes groove the plant-foot-next-to-ball pattern so touches stop being random.

steps.dose: 3 × 30 m at 60/80/95%, then 3 shots at 80% with hips leading the swing
steps.why: Graded intensity primes sprint speed and the hip-first striking chain, and protects the airways.

pregame.anchorCue: Before the ball comes: check your shoulder, then show your tripod.
pregame.airwayNote: Continuous running in cool air is a strong EIB trigger. The variable-intensity build-up runs are your airway warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Keep HR ~160-185 in short bursts, walk between. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static stretches before
Hard shooting before the legs are warm
Full-speed sprints in the first 2 minutes
pregame.teachMe: Soccer is a balance sport disguised as a running sport: the plant leg decides how cleanly force reaches the ball. Your flat feet make the plant leg wobble, so the drills set the arch and lock the knee over the foot before any ball work.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Calms the grip-everything threat response so strokes stay loose, and primes recruitment for the first explosive step.

steps.dose: 10 tossed balls tracked to the strings of a racket held still, then 20 s following a moving ball with eyes only
steps.why: Fear of the ball shows up as eyes leaving early. Watching easy balls all the way onto the strings teaches the brain the ball is safe.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 3 × 8 split-step pogos landing in ready (knees ~25°, hips ~15°)
steps.why: The split-step is an elastic pre-load. Stiff ankles plus an arched foot mean the push-off happens instantly instead of after a sag.

steps.dose: 8 Hip Snaps with racket across chest, then 8 shadow strokes each side: hips turn first, racket last
steps.why: Your arm fires first. Hip Snaps install ground → hips → trunk → arm so the racket head is the fastest link, which fixes balls flying long or into the net.

steps.dose: 3 shadow swings each at low / waist / high contact, then 6 lateral shuffles, stick 1 s, swing
steps.why: Reference swings calibrate contact height; sticking each set-up position replaces reaching and lunging with moving the feet first.

steps.dose: 1 min mini-tennis, 2 min baseline at 70 → 90%
steps.why: Gradual ramp maps the installed pattern onto real balls before points count.

pregame.anchorCue: Between points: split-step bounce, eyes on the opponent's strings.
pregame.airwayNote: Tennis is intermittent high intensity, which suits an interval-style warm-up: the split-step pogos and rally ramp provide it (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Short bursts to HR ~165-180. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Long static shoulder or hamstring stretches before
Max-effort serves in the first 3 minutes
Changing grip or technique on match day
pregame.teachMe: A groundstroke is a rotation transfer from the floor to the racket. Each body segment accelerates and then brakes so the next one goes faster. If the arm starts it, contact gets random because the arm is doing a job the hips should do. Installing hip-first now means you don't have to think about it during the match.

steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Pickleball punishes tension: a gripping body pops the ball up. The exhale releases the brake; the isometric wakes up recruitment for fast hands.

steps.dose: 10 soft tosses toward your face that you block with a still paddle, then 20 s near-far (paddle face → far baseline)
steps.why: Hands battles at the kitchen trigger the flinch. Blocking easy balls teaches the brain an incoming ball is safe, which speeds up reactions.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, then hold ready position 60 s (knees ~25°, hip hinge ~15°, paddle up, weight slightly forward)
steps.why: Holding the exact ready angles for 60 s installs the position so you default to it instead of standing tall and reaching.

steps.dose: 3 shadow strokes each at low (dink), chest (block), overhead; then 6 side shuffles to a dink, stick 1 s
steps.why: Reference strokes calibrate paddle angle per height. Sticking each shuffle installs feet-first instead of lunging.

steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, then 6 shadow drives with hips leading
steps.why: Drives and overheads go long when the arm leads. Hip-first turns the paddle into the end of a whip.

steps.dose: 1 min dinks, 1 min drives at 70 → 90%
steps.why: Puts real balls on the installed pattern before points count.

pregame.anchorCue: Between points: paddle up, sit into ready.
avoid: Static stretching before
Smashing at 100% in the first minute
pregame.teachMe: At the kitchen, the winner is usually whoever is already in position. Ready position puts your center of mass over a wide, arched base so the first move needs no wind-up. Eyes that aren't afraid of the ball pick up the opponent's paddle angle earlier, which buys you time you don't feel but you'll see.

steps.drill: Box breathing + wall push isometric (acceleration lean)
steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push in a 45° sprint lean, one knee driven up
steps.why: The lean isometric rehearses the exact acceleration angle and recruits more high-threshold units.

steps.dose: 20 s near-far, then pick one point at the finish and lock eyes on it for 3 breaths
steps.why: A steady gaze keeps the head still, which keeps the trunk still, which keeps force going straight back into the track.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 20 pogos, 2 × 15 m A-skips
steps.why: Sprinting is elastic: short ground contacts depend on a stiff Achilles and an arch that doesn't collapse. Pogos tune that spring right before you need it.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 wall-drill switches, 3 falling starts into 10 m
steps.why: Grooves the push-back-and-down force direction of acceleration so the first three steps aren't wasted upward.

steps.dose: 3 × 30-40 m at 70/85/95%, full walk-back rest
steps.why: Ramps the nervous system to race speed and acts as an interval warm-up for the airways.

pregame.anchorCue: In the blocks or stance: push the ground away.
pregame.airwayNote: Short sprints are less of an EIB trigger than long runs, but the warm-up still matters: interval/variable-intensity warm-ups reduced post-exercise lung-function drop (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B), protection roughly 1-2 h. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Static stretching before
Max sprints before a full warm-up
Heavy lifting earlier the same day
pregame.teachMe: Sprint speed = how much force you can put into the ground during a very short contact, and in which direction. A flat foot lengthens contact time because the arch has to sag before it can push. The pogos and Screw shorten that window so more of each contact becomes forward propulsion.

steps.dose: 3 breaths, then 2 × 6 s wall push
steps.why: Lowers threat arousal so passing arms stay quiet instead of swinging at the ball.

steps.dose: 10 tosses toward your chest received on still forearms
steps.why: Watching the ball onto a still platform kills the flinch that sends passes everywhere.

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 15 pogos, 30 s ready position (knees ~25°, hips ~15°, weight forward)
steps.why: Sets an arched, stiff base so the first move to the ball is instant.

steps.drill: Approach Step-and-Stick + Hip Snap arm swing
steps.dose: 4 approaches landing two-footed and freezing 1 s, then 6 standing arm swings where the hips open before the arm
steps.why: Freezing the landing installs safe knee alignment for flat feet; hip-first arm swings make hits harder and less random.

steps.dose: 3 approach jumps at 70/85/95%, then 5 hits at 80%
steps.why: Ramps elastic loading and the hitting chain before game speed.

pregame.anchorCue: Before the serve: bounce once, land in ready.
avoid: Static stretching before
Max jumps or full-speed spikes in the first minutes
pregame.teachMe: A spike is a vertical jump plus a whip. The jump depends on an elastic, stiff base, and the hit depends on the order the segments fire. Get the foot and the order right before the first point, so the game just runs the pattern.

steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push in fight stance
steps.why: Threat state shows up as freezing under strikes. A long, controlled breath tells the nervous system the situation is safe enough to see clearly; the isometric primes full recruitment.

steps.dose: 10 slow glove/hand pushes toward your face that you watch and parry (sibling or wall), then 20 s soft-focus on the chest while noticing hands at the edges
steps.why: Eyes closing or turning away on incoming strikes is the core fear response. Slow, safe approaches recalibrate it before contact.

steps.drill: The Screw in stance + level-change pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw in stance, 2 × 10 pogos into a sprawl-ready level change
steps.why: A rooted, arched stance stops the knee caving and lets force travel from the floor into punches and shots.

steps.drill: Hip Snap → jab-cross shadow + Step-and-Stick level change
steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, 1 round (60 s) shadow jab-cross with hips leading, 4 penetration steps freezing 1 s at the bottom
steps.why: Installs ground → hips → shoulder → fist and a balanced shot entry, so your arm stops punching alone.

steps.dose: 2 × 30 s at 70% → 90% (mitts with sibling at contact-ladder level 1, or shadow), 2 sprawls
steps.why: Ramps intensity without fatigue. At home with your younger sibling stay on contact-ladder levels 0-2: shadow, pads, cooperative drilling.

pregame.anchorCue: Between exchanges: exhale through the nose, chin down, tripod feet.
pregame.airwayNote: Rounds are interval efforts, so the ramp above doubles as a variable-intensity airway warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Bursts to HR ~170-190, recover between. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Hard sparring as a warm-up
Static stretching before
Learning a brand-new technique right before live rounds
Above contact-ladder level 2 with your younger sibling
pregame.teachMe: Power in a strike is not arm strength: it's how fast and in what order you transfer force from the floor. Each link speeds up then brakes to fling the next. Fear narrows vision and makes you grip, which slows every link. Calm eyes plus a rooted foot is the fastest path to a harder, cleaner punch.

steps.drill: Downshift breathing + wall push isometric (shot angle)
steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s wall push in a low penetration-step angle
steps.why: Rehearses the drive angle at max intent and calms the gripping response that makes you stiff in ties.

steps.dose: 30 s: eyes soft on a partner's (or imagined) hips while tracking hand movement in peripheral vision
steps.why: Hips don't fake; watching them with a wide field lets you react to level changes earlier.

steps.drill: The Screw in stance + level-change pogos
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw in stance, 2 × 10 small hops dropping into stance on landing
steps.why: Sets an arched foot and stiff ankles so the shot leaves from the floor instead of from bent-over arms.

steps.dose: 6 penetration steps freezing 1 s at the bottom, 6 hip escapes (shrimps) each way
steps.why: Freezing at the bottom installs head-up, hips-under alignment; shrimps groove the escape pattern with no thought needed.

steps.dose: 3 shots at 70/85/95% speed, 3 sprawls
steps.why: Ramps to match speed and doubles as an interval warm-up. With your younger sibling stay on contact-ladder levels 0-2.

pregame.anchorCue: Reset in stance: tripod feet, hips under.
pregame.airwayNote: Wrestling is anaerobic intervals with hard breathing, an EIB trigger. The shot/sprawl ramp is your variable-intensity warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Bursts to HR ~175-190. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Live goes as a warm-up
Static stretching before
Neck bridges at max load before matches
pregame.teachMe: A takedown wins at the floor: the drive comes from feet pushing back so the hips go forward. A collapsing arch angles that push sideways. Lock the base, then rehearse the shape at full speed once, so the match just replays it.

steps.drill: Box breathing + wall push isometric in stance
steps.dose: 3 cycles 4-4-4-4, then 2 × 6 s wall push from your boxing stance (rear hand)
steps.why: A long exhale turns off the flinch/freeze reflex; the max isometric from stance primes the exact chain you'll punch with.

steps.dose: 10 slow glove/hand pushes toward your face (sibling or wall partner) that you watch until the last moment and parry, then 6 slow slips keeping eyes open
steps.why: Blinking or looking away on punches is the threat response. Slow, safe approaches teach the brain to keep the eyes open, which is the start of all defense.

steps.drill: The Screw in stance + pogos in stance
steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 2 × 15 small bounce pogos in stance
steps.why: Arched feet and a springy ankle let you push off for footwork and drive the ground into the punch.

steps.drill: Hip Snap → jab-cross shadow with Step-and-Stick
steps.dose: 6 Hip Snaps, then 1 round (90 s) shadow: step in, jab-cross, stick 1 s balanced, step out
steps.why: Installs ground → hips → shoulder → fist; the 1 s freeze makes sure you finish every combo on balance instead of falling in.

steps.dose: 2 × 45 s at 70% → 90% (pads with sibling at contact-ladder level 1, or shadow)
steps.why: Ramps speed and heart rate without fatigue. At home with your younger sibling: contact-ladder levels 0-2 only.

pregame.anchorCue: Between rounds: long exhale, chin down, bounce.
pregame.airwayNote: Rounds are interval efforts; this ramp doubles as a variable-intensity airway warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Bursts to HR ~170-190, recover between. Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Hard sparring as a warm-up
Static stretches before
Max-power bag work before technique
Above contact-ladder level 2 with your younger sibling
pregame.teachMe: A cross is a chain: the back foot pushes the floor, the hip turns, the trunk turns, the shoulder fires and the fist lands last. Each link has to brake to hand speed to the next one. If the arm starts first, the big engines never contribute. Calm eyes give you the time to throw it right.

steps.dose: 3 breaths (4 s in, 6 s out), then 2 × 6 s max-intent bridge press against the floor
steps.why: BJJ rewards calm. A long exhale prevents the panic-grip that burns your arms out in the first roll.

steps.dose: 20 s soft gaze noticing the whole room, then 20 s eyes closed doing slow shrimps
steps.why: Grappling relies on feel as much as sight; eyes-closed movement sharpens body position sense (proprioception).

steps.dose: 3 × 5 s Screw, 6 bridges, 6 shrimps each side
steps.why: Hip-driven movement starts from the feet. Setting the foot tripod makes bridges and escapes powerful instead of arm-pushes.

steps.dose: 4 technical stand-ups each side, 4 hip escapes freezing 1 s on the frame
steps.why: Freezing at the end of each escape installs the frame-then-hip order.

steps.dose: 2 × 60 s at 50% → 80% (cooperative; with sibling stay at contact-ladder levels 0-2)
steps.why: Gradually loads grip and breathing before live rounds.

pregame.airwayNote: Long rolls can trigger EIB. The flow-roll ramp is a variable-intensity warm-up (Stickland 2012 systematic review, grade B; protection roughly 1-2 h). Use your prescribed pre-exercise inhaler as your doctor set it up.
avoid: Max-effort rolls as a warm-up
Neck cranks or heavy neck bridges before rolling
Above contact-ladder level 2 with your younger sibling; tap early

items.note: French contrast: heavy, plyo, loaded-plyo, assisted/fast — rests short within, long between.

items.dose: 2 × 6–8 per side, phase tempo applied

items.dose: 2 × 4 (phases 1–2 only)

rules: Phase 1 — Eccentric (2–3 wk): slow 4–5 s lowerings on the main lift only.
Phase 2 — Isometric (2 wk): 2–3 s pauses at the sticking point.
Phase 3 — Concentric/Explosive (2 wk): normal lowering, max-intent up, lighter-ish loads.
Phase 4 — French Contrast (2–3 wk): heavy → plyo → loaded plyo → fast plyo.
Deload a week between blocks or when a game-dense week hits.
